PUBLIC AND PRIVATE BILLS- QUESTIONS OF ORDER.
speechtext:
Upon the motion, yesterday, by the hon. member for Thunder Bay and Rainy River for leave to introduce a Bill intituled an Act to amend chapter 139, 4 and 5, Edward VII., intituled ' An Act respecting the Ontario and Minnesota Power Company, Limited,' I stated that I would to-day give a more extensive opinion upon his right to introduce the Bill as a public measure.
Upon a careful perusal of the proposed Bill I find that it is composed entirely of amendments to sections of the Act incorporating the Ontario and Minnesota Power Company, Limited, the main provisions being as follows :
To compel the company to provide further plans and execute additional work and carry out any new works required by such authority as may have jurisdiction on the Rainy river at or near Fort Frances, and that if, upon the application of the town or otherwise, it appears that the company has executed any work not approved by the Governor in Council the company shall, if directed, carry out any work or make any change required, and also with regard to the flow of water through the works of the company, the supply of power and energy, and the regulation of the methods and conditions under which the same shall be furnished and the prices therefor. And, further, that the company shall deliver, in Canada, a stated proportion of the total power delivered by them, and that the town of Fort Frances may, if a resolution of its council represents that the determination of the quantity of power, prices, conditions and manner of service of electrical power and energy is important in the interests of the town, apply to the Board of Railway Commissioners, which shall determine such application.
As to whether certain portions of the Bill are, or are not, properly the subject of a public Act is not necessary for me to determine, but upon the extracts from the Bill which I have just given I would state the following opinions from authorities. It is stated by Bourinot, 3rd edition, page 706, that:
Private Bills are distinguished from public Bills in that they directly relate to the affair?

speechtext:
of private individuals or of corporate bodies, and not to matters of public policy or to the community in general.
And at page 728:
'Bills from the corporations of towns and municipal bodies, generally, are always treated as private Bills when they desire special legislation affecting their property or interests.
And on page 729, Bourinot states as follows:
As a rule, it may be stated that when Bills treat of matters of general pdlicy, such as sanitary, or police, or commercial, or fiscal regulations, they may be considered as public measures. In fact, >alll Bills affecting the general interests of the community, and involving considerations of public policy, are out of the category of private Bills dealing with the special interests of corporations or associations.
May 6th edition, page 626, says:
Every Bill for the particular interest or benefit of any person or persons, is treated as a private Bill. Whether it be for the interest of an individual, a public company or corporation, a parish, a city, a county, or other locality, it is equally distinguished from a measure of public policy, in which the whole community are interested.
Even in England the most extreme case in which a Bill affecting local interests has been admitted as a public Bill is in the case of the metropolis of London, where such Bills have frequently been held to be public Bills by reason of the large area and vast population and the variety of interests concerned, thus constituting them measures of public policy rather than of focal interest.
This cannot be'said to be the present case.
Ilbert's Legislative Methods and Forms (1901), at page 28 says:
A private Bill is a measure for the interest of some person or class of persons, whether an individual, a corporation, or the Inhabitants of a county, town, parish or other locality, and originates on the petition of the person or persons interested. A public Bill is introduced as a measure of public policy in which the whole comm unity is interested, and originates on the motion of some member of the House in which the Bill is introduced.
And on page 30:
Bills relating to particular localities only are, as a rule, treated as private Bills.
In view of the nature of the Bill proposed by the hon. member, and of the precedents (among which are those which I have already quoted) I must hold that the Bill is a private Bill, and must be introduced as such and must comply with the rules of the House respecting private Bills.

Mr. Speaker, before the House goes into Committee of Supply, I would like to call the attention of the government to proceedings which are now pending before the United States Congress for conferring powers upon a company which proposes to construct a darn across the River St. Lawrence near what is known as the Long Sault. We have in Canada what may be fairly described as the greatest system of inland waterways in the world, and every one of us, I think, realizes that the River St. Lawrence is not only an important, but a vital portion of that system of waterways. The Prime Minister is no doubt thoroughly aware that under the treaty between Great Britain and the United States which was negotiated and ratified in 1842, it was provided by article VII. as follows:
It is further agreed that the channels in the River St. Lawrence on both sides of the Long Sault islands and of Barnhart island, the channels in the River Detroit, on both sides of the Island Bois Blanc, and between that island and both the Canadian and American shores, and all the several channels and passages between the various islands lying near the junction of the River St. Clair with the lake of that name, shall be equally free and open to the ships, vessels and boats of both parties.
So that the channels of the River St. Lawrence, from shore to shore, at the particular point which I have mentioned, are, under the terms of this treaty, to remain forever open to both nations. The country was rather disturbed by a proposal which was brought before this House during the last session of parliament, to grant to certain gentlemen authority to construct that portion of the dam across the River St Lawrence which would lie in Canadian waters.
There was no such proposal as that before parliament last session.
Well, I have an entirely different recollection in that regard from that of my hon. friend.	*
My hon. friend has not read the Bill, I am afraid. [DOT]

I read the Bill and debated it. The hon. gentleman is very ready to rise and interrupt and contradict. He is no more correct on this occasion than he has been on several occasions in the immediate past. The proposal that was laid before parliament last session involved the damming of the River St. Lawrence, according to my opinion of what that proposal really meant. I shall not go over that argument again. I stated my apprehension of what the proposal was at the time. The mere fact that the hon. gentleman entertains a different view of the proposal does not justify him in making the fiat contradiction which he did a moment ago.
The legislature of the state of New York passed an Act, I do not know just at what date, which confers certain powers upon a company that had been organized in the United States. I believe that the real promoter of that measure is a very wealthy and powerful company in the United States called the Aluminium Company. The state of New York was not able to give to the promoters the complete powers which they desired, and there is now a Bill before the Congress of the United States which is designed to round out and complete the powers, so that this company may have absolute authority, so far as the state of New York and the Congress of the United States can give it, to dam the River St. Lawrence. I appreciate thoroughly, of course, the fact that we retain jurisdiction over our own portion of the bed of the River St. Lawrence, notwithstanding anything that the Congress of the United States may enact. This company proposes to develop about 500,000 horse-power. That is to be developed for purely manufacturing purposes, and I find in the measure a reasonable enough provision, if it were to go through, that at least half of this power shall be for use in the United States, and that no more than half of the total power generated by the complete works shall be employed or used in Canada. The Bill now before Congress has been opposed by a great many Canadian interests, as I am informed. I find, from a brief which has been filed in ' opposition to this Bill, that memorials have been filed before the Committee of Congress by the International Waterways Commission, the board of trade of the city of Toronto, the Dominion Marine Association, the Montreal board of trade, La Chambre de Com-

meree du District of Montreal, the Commission for Conservation of Canada, the Ontario government by its attorney I. Hillard, K.C., and Geo. C. Bolt, for the New York Board of Trade, all in opposition to the Bill. The Bill proposes, as I understand from this brief-because I have not been able to secure an authentic copy of the Bill except so far as it has been published in the press of the country-in the first place, a channel and a lock on the American side, and, in the next place, a complete dam across both channels. Of course, it is realized that authority to construct that portion of the dam across the Canadian portion of the channel must come from this parliament. The project includes all that, and this company has obtained from the state of New York and is in process of obtaining from the Congress of the United States the authority that will enable it by and by to come to this parliament and say, we now invite you to give us authority to make this connecting link for the purpose of developing this enormous power. I was rather struck by one sentence in the report of the Committee of Congress which had this Bill under consideration. That committee has favourably reported upon the Bill, and it now stands in Congress upon that favourable report. One sentence in that report I may quote as informing this House and this country of one powerful reason why that Bill has commended itself to the Committee of Congress. That sentence is this; the proposal of the company to furnish a suitable channel for commerce entirely in American territory. The dam will go completely across the river, from shore to shore, and the proposal is that the channel shall be entirely in American territory, the suggestion being that this will be a very much more advantageous situation for the people of the United States than that which exists at the present time.
Now this company undertakes to do very wonderful things. In the preamble of this Bill now before Congress it is said that, among other things, it is for the purpose of improving the navigaton of the St. Lawrence; and in the first section of the Bill there is the declaration that the purposes of the corporation include the permanent improvement of the navigation of the St. Lawrence at above or below such place. The government of Canada up to the present has followed the policy, and I hope will persevere in it, that the navigation of the St. Lawrence is of such paramount importance that it ought not to be confided to private interests, but should be kept absolutely under the control of the people as represented by parliament. But it appears that the navigation of that river shall be confided in a certain measure at least, to the great and powerful company which is
behind those proposals. I do not propose to go at any length into the dangers of the Bill now before the American Congress; but I may say, quoting from the brief which has been filed in opposition to that/ Bill, that Mr. John Kennedy, of Montreal, a very skilful and experenced engineer, appeared as a witness on behalf of the Montreal Board of Harbour Commissioners. Mr. Kennedy is an engineer of very well known ability, character and experience. He lives upon the St. Lawrence and has made it a life study, more particularly as regards its navigation, and he did not hesitate to express the opinion that the project, upon the facts disclosed, would result in an impairment of navigation instead of an improvement. Two captains and pilots, who have been engaged for years in the navigation of the St. Lawrence, both upon freight and passenger vessels, joined in expressing the same opinion. The brief goes on further to state that the experience of the Canadian government in an energetic effort to improve navigation at the Galop rapids, is conclusive demonstration of the fact that it is impossible to tell in advance what effect an obstruction of this kind would have on the navigation of that river:
The Canadian government, under the advice of its best engineers, expended $1,100,000 in an attempt to improve navigation at the Gallop rapids for the last few years.
And I am merely quoting the brief when I say that the experiment has not proved a very great success and has not justified the anticipations which were formed with regard to it. Now it is stated further in this brief, and I commend this to the House a3 an opinion to which some weight might be attached:
It is impossible for either engineers or pilots to state precisely what the result of the project would be as to navigation. The probabilities only can be suggested. The project once authorized, the investment once made, if the result is disastrous to navigation, the public will have to bear it, except on the condition of reimbursing the company for its investments.
Further than that, this proposal is said by the report of this commission to be probably subject-in all probability subject- to the sanction of the InternationalJYater-ways Commission. It is perfectly time that one clause of the Bill does expressly state, according to the press report, that the said Long Sault Development Company, its successors and assignees shall be subject to the provisions of the treaty between the United States and Great Britain relative to the boundary waters between the United States and Canada, proclaimed by the President of the United States on the 13th July, 1910. But is not made expressly subject to the provision of the Ashburton

treaty, and the provisions of that treaty are much more vitally important to the people in that regard than are the provisions of the treaty to which allusion is made in the Bill now before Congress. The danger of ice dams is also pointed out in this brief, tout as that was discussed last year, I shall not go into it to-day except to say that it is one which ought__not to be lost sight of by the government.
I have spoken so far altogether of the danger which may result to our great system of inland waterways, but it seems _ to me there is possibly another aspect which should not be lost sight of. We know the importance of our water-powers to-day in Canada, and we shall realize more thoroughly in years to come their exceeding great value. They are not like supplies of coal and iron and other natural resources of this country, which are dissipated in, the user. Our water-powers are permanent and enduring, and their value is likely to be much greater in the future. What are we to do with them? Should we preserve them for the benefit of the whole people of Canada or hand them over to the control of a great private corporation and an alien corporation at that ? I think it would be madness for this country to consent to the latter alternative. I go further. When a project of this kind has been put forward on the other side of the line and has already received the sanction of the state_ of New York and is now asking the sanction of Congress, this government, not only on account of the danger of the impairment of the navigation of the St. Lawrence and our system of inland waterways, tout for the purpose of protecting the great water-powers of this country and seeing that they are developed in the interests of the whole people, ought to take energetic measures to make known their views in this regard. The development of these water-powers, if ever undertaken, should only be undertaken subject to the paramount importance of our system of inland waterways^ If it can be undertaken without the slightest danger of impairment to that great system, it ought to be undertaken by or under the control of this government so that these natural resources of immense value now, and of infinitely greater value in the future, should be conserved for the 'benefit of the whole people of Canada. Therefore I thought it right to bring these facts to the notice of parliament, even in this very brief and somewhat fragmentary way, and to ask the government -whether in the first place they have taken any steps, or propose to take any, to safeguard the interests of navigation, and in the second place to make it perfectly plain that this country does not intend to commit itself to any scheme by which these enormously valuable natural resources shall be handed over to a private corporation ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Every one is aware that this is a subject regarding which, ever since it has been called to the attention of the country, there is_ quite a serious nervousness in public opinion as to the consequences which might flow from the intended works to which my hon. friend has just alluded. In fact I believe that the nervousness existing has been beyond the cause-natural and legitimate as it was -and what should have been the effect of such a cause. I believe that in many instances it has prejudged the opinion even of members of the House. And in this I would not exclude even my hon. friend, because, if I understood him aright, he has just expressed again the opinion which he expressed last session, that the Bill had the effect of authorizing the damming of the St. Lawrence. My opinion is different from that expressed bv my hon. friend. Reading the Bill in cold blood, whatever may have been intended afterwards, it seems clear that the effect of the Bill of last session was simply to authorize a transmission line and nothing else.
I am speaking of the Bill as introduced.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Even the Bill as introduced, I think I am right in saying, related to a transmission line only. But my hon. friend (Mr. Borden, Halifax) and many other members of the House saw in this transmission line Bill something nefarious, they saw a scheme to block the St. Lawrence. And even in the observations my hon. friend has just addressed to the House, he shows that he still looks upon this measure as implying the damming of the St. Lawrence from shore to shore. Speaking for myself, at all events, before the government of the day would agree to such a proposal there would be very ample discussion in this House and a good deal more information than we have upon the matter at the present time. I understand that the men, especially in the city of Montreal, who are primarily interested in this question, seek to block this measure at every step because they fear that the ultimate object is to throw a bar across the St. Lawrence from shore to shore.	.	,
The Bill to which my hon. friend referred a moment ago was first introduced in the legislature of the state of New York and passed. It was afterwards introduced in the federal legislature at Washington and has, I understand, taken its preliminary stages. So far as I am aware-and, at present, my information concerning it is simply from the public prints-it deals only with the southern channel-
The South Sault.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
That channel is undoubtedly in American territory. Now, let us take the first step in this matter.

The channel is in American territory; my understanding of international law is that a sovereign power has the right, in the case of an international stream such as this, to place upon its own shore of that stream all works which it deems for its own advantage, being limited alone by the necessity, as in this case particularly, of not doing anything which would affect navigation.
Would not the damming of the South Sault impair navigation?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
That is not
the question at the present time; I am considering only the principle of international law. The Americans, as I understand it, have the right to use that stream in any way they please, but they are not to do anything to impair navigation.
Under treaty.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Yes. That is the general principle of international law, but is still more true in this case because of the treaty of 1842. But, Sir, if a nation, under such circumstances, does anything which, in the opinion of the nation on the other side of the stream, impairs navigation, who is to decide? Under international law there is no tribunal to settle the point whether it is or is not an impairment of navigation; and the only remedy under such circumstances would be for the party who thinks that the work does impair navigation to appeal to the honour and honesty of the other side.
The Ashburton treaty covers that point fairly. It states there must be ' free navigation,' so the sovereign right of the United States is given up.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That is what I said. But I was pointing out that if the United States puts up a work on its side of the stream which in our opinion, impairs navigation but in their opinion does not impair navigation, who is to decide? If it were a provincial or national stream in our own territory, the matter would go before the courts. But the hon. gentleman knows that, while we have principles of international law well known and generally recognized by the nations, there is, up to this moment, no tribunal to see to the observance of these principles. The only arbitrament we have is that of war. But we can do this,-we can protest and appeal to the other side and represent that this is an interference with our treaty rights.
Would not the Ashburton treaty cover that?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Is not the Ashburton treaty the last arbitration treaty-yes ; I was just coming, or had just come to that. While nations generally have no arbitrament in such matters we have constituted a tribunal to cover these points. So, this law of Congress, if it passes, would be passed over our protest,, and the matter must be submitted to the court we have constituted under the Waterways treaty.
I may say that we on our side of the St. Lawrence have erected works, which, to. some extent may interfere with navigation, but not to such an extent as to cause remonstrance on the other side?
Where are these?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I think that ' the dam at Sheik island is one. I do not know to what extent it may interfere with navigation, but in some respects, it is beneficial. No protest has been made. I put this by way of illustration. We have taken it upon ourselves to disturb the channel as nature made it.
When we heard of this Bill being introduced at Washington, we put ourselves into communication with the British jimbassa-dor to remonstrate; and correspondence is going on now upon the subject. I expect that we shall have an official copy of the Bill at a very early day. I may say that I was informed that the Bill reported from the committee in charge of the same is considerably different from the Bill as introduced. However that may be, we have taken steps to have the whole correspondence laid before us, and as soon as we receive it it will be our duty at once to lay it before the House.
Have the government consulted in this matter with the government of Ontario or the Hydro-Electric Commission?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No, we have not come to the point of consulting anybody. We have not the measure before us-.
Is it the intention to consult

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: We will decide that when we have the Bill.
Apparently, the International Waterways Commission, under the treaty, will have a great deal of power in deciding this matter. If they decide it, will that put it beyond the power of this House?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I am afraid that the question of works to be constructed in the United States is beyond the jurisdiction of this House.

But they know that under the treaty they cannot affect the height of the water on the other side without having the approval of both countries. So if they dammed the Sault, and it had the effect of raising the height of water on the Canadian side, we would have something to say about it What I wanted to know is if this

commission took the matter up and decided that a dam there was permissible, would this parliament cease to have any control over the subject?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That is a question of law. I would not be prepared to say.

A very important question. There is one thing we must consider. There is no American interest that would suffer at all if this approval was granted. The only interests to suffer on either side are Canadian interests. You cannot put your finger on a single solitary American interest but that would gain by damming the river there. Now, look at the condition of things in the New England states. The large manufacturing centres thatl have been using water-power, and where they have denuded the country of timber, now find that a continuous water supply is failing them. There exists now a great deal of apprehension in the eastern states in manufacturing districts on this very point. The whole object of this undertaking is, if possible, to get control of that river for the development of electrical power, and to transmit that power to all that eastern section of the country, where the larger manufacturing centres of the United States exist. Now, we know that if they get control of that power and transmit it to these centres to build up their manufactories, it will be impossible for Canada ever to get back their share of that power, if they once let it go. Now these are questions certainly of vital interest to the Canadian people. I speak from a local knowledge of the circumstances. We' know that engineers, with all their intelligence, sometimes make great mistakes; they have made great mistakes in this country within a short time. No one can tell what effect that dam might have upon the general interest of navigation in this country; we do not know anything about it. It seems to me that if a commission is to be allowed to deal with this matter, they should have at least the most thorough knowledge of the local conditions before they do anything. 1 live in a locality that will be seriously affected by this dam, at least that is the apprehension, and for that 'reason I did not wish to allow this matter to pass without savins something.

There is one phase of this question that has not been touched on. When it was up for discussion a year ago, it was pointed out that in 1901 this House gave the St. Lawrence Power Company authority to dam the St. Lawrence river at this particular point. That com-panv was partly Canadian and partly Mr. BRODER.
American, but afterwards the charter was assigned to a totally American company. All that company require at the present time is the approval of the Minister of Public Works to the plans that they may submit to this government, in order to enable them to build a dam across the St. Lawrence river at this point. It was stated by one of the men\ interested in the Bill that was before the House last year, that they were going to get the authority, they were going to build a dam, and they would give Canada 90 days in which to take up one-half the power, and if it was not taken up within that period, the whole power would be sent to New York, the idea being to send it to New York city. What I would like to be sure about is that this company cannot get the right to dam the St. Lawrence by getting the approval and authority of the present Waterways Commission. I would like to have the assurance of the Prime Minister that was given last year, that before anything is done on that line to enable this company, or any other company, to dam the St. Lawrence, before any plans are approved, or authority is given, there shall be an opportunity for ample discussion of the whole matter in the House of Commons.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Hear, hear.

Perhaps we had better get a clear understanding of the position we are in. What are our legal rights in reference to this matter? The hon. member who has just spoken (Mr. Turriff) says that in 1901 power was given by this parliament to some company to dam the river. My contention is that under the Ashburton treaty no government in this country can give power to a private company to do anything of the kind; that power must come directly from the parliament of Canada. Have we the right to delegate all our powers to this International Waterways Commission? I saw it stated when the Bill was introduced in the United States that this legislation must be subject to the approval of the International Commission. Have we given our powers to that commission that we exercise under the Ashburton treaty? If we have, then that commission have the power of approval of a project to erect the construction provided for by that Bill. As I understand the agreement between the two governments, they have both given to this International Commission the approval of works of this kind. I need not dwell upon the necessity of this work, I spoke upon it before in the House. I have a strong view that this spot is perhaps one of the most beautiful in Canada, and it ought to be preserved to the people of Canada for all generations. Its value

to Canadians from an aesthetic point of view will be greater than its value as a source of electrical power. How much the proposition will interfere with navigation, we know not. I think perhaps improvements could be made on that stream of such a character that they would not interfere with the use of the river for navigation. But I protest as a Canadian against the damming of the river at that beautiful spot, and using it solely as a purpose of acquiring wealth. My ideas may be perhaps not sufficiently utilitarian, not up to the ideals of the present day, but such as they are I gave them to the House. I did not know that the Act passed by this House in 1901 had the wide power the hon. gentleman says it had. I do not remember any such Bill passing the House, I doubt very much if it gave such power. It may be a Bill empowering them to do some kind of work, but I do not think there is anything on our statute-book transferring this property absolutely to them. The control of that is entirely in our hands. We have not interfered with the navigation in any way on our side. We have improved the navigation. The erection of the Sheik's island dam for the purpose of improving navigation has interfered in no way with any right that the Americans had under the Ashburton treaty. It was improving and utilizing the river for the purpose of navigation and not for the purpose of interfering with it at all. That is a right which we have exercised from time immemorial and can. Finally, let us keep that, one of the beauty spots of the country, for the benefit of the whole people of Canada, not devoting it to the utilitarian purpose of generating 500,000 or 600,000 horse-power, but keeping it to look upon, if for nothing else.
Did I understand the Prime Minister to say that he had already protested to British Ambassador Bryce against the passage of this Bill in Washington?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: We made representations-yes.

With reference to the understanding of the Prime Minister that this is simply to dam what is called the South Sault, I have (before me the Bill which was passed in New York state, and which is being confirmed in Washington, and they are asking for power.
To construct, maintain and operate for water-power and other purposes a dam or dams across the St. Lawrence river between points on the United States and Canadian shores of said river near Long Sault island, or Barnhart's island or Sheik's island.
And to the international boundary.

To the international boundary line. So, it is not through what is known as the South Sault. The Prime Minister also stated that we had practically violated the Ashburton treaty when we had built what is known as the Sheik's island dam.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I did not say that. I said that we had interfered with nature.

Sheik's island dam is below the head of the canal, so that there was no waterway. There might have been a little water running through but there was no navigation of any kind. The Ashburton treaty says that neither government must interfere with navigation between Sheik's island, and the American shore, and Sheik's island is on the Canadian side. If there had been navigation between Sheik's island and the Canadian shore we would have been interfering with the Ashburton treaty.
What are the words of the Ashburton treaty?

They are not just exactly as they are construed in this discussion. The words are as follows :
It is further 'agreed that the channels in the River St. Lawrence on both sides of the Long Sault islands and of Barnhart island; the channels in the River Detroit op both sides of the Island Bois Blanc, and between that island and both the American and Canadian shores; and all the several channels and passages between the varions islands lying near the junction of the River St. Clair with the lake of that name, shall be equallj free and open to the ships, vessels and boats of both parties.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That is to say that in the Canadian channel the Americans have the right of navigation, and in the American channel the 'Canadians have the right of navigation.
Yes.

The Ashburton treaty says that the channels in the St. Lawrence river are free to both parties. There is not any channel on the other side of Sheik's island. The whole channel is at Long Sault and at Barnhart's island. This South Sault channel that they propose to dam is a navigable stream, and is used every day. It is the channel that freight- boats are going down every day ; not very large freight boats, but steamers 100 feet long and 20 feet wide run down through there. They carry probably 100 tons. Then, the rafts all go down through the South Sault, and they have been running down there for fifty or one hundred years. The smaller pleasure steamers go down there. If they dam that channel, I understand the right hon. Prime Min-

ister believes that the north side would then ibe all right for those large steamers like the Richelieu Navigation Company's steamers. But the damming of the South Sault is sure to raise the water many feet. I suppose the effect will be to raise it 40 feet. Thus, it will throw the water into the North Sault and spoil that channel. That is the impression of marine men. They have led the Prime Minister to believe that all they propose to do is to erect this dam but, once that channel is spoiled, you might as well let them go on and do as they like.

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Reid,	Grenville) understands	the	local
conditions, and I would like him to explain. I understand that the Bill provides that this company shall have the right to extend dams as far northward as the international boundary line?
Mr.	REID (Grenville).	Yes.Mr.	LENNOX. That	would	cross	over
from the shore to Barnhart's island, and then to Long Sault island.
Mr.	REID (Grenville).	And	then	from
IiOng Sault to Shiek's island.
And the international boundary is north of Sheik's island.
No Sheik's island is on the Canadian side.
Well, that would extend their dam <as far north as Long Sault island before they would come to the international boundary?
It would extend it to Sheik's island dam which would be the international boundary.
The international boundary is south of Sheik's .island.
Yes.
In doing that would they not be cutting off the only available channel there is now?

We would only have a small part of the stream. At that particular point where they want to construct the dam practically the whole of the river is on the American side. The South Sault is entirely on the American side.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It is a question for the engineers as to what would be the effect of this work. The Bill which is now under consideration at Washington does not, as the hon. gentleman has stated quite incorrectly, provide for the creation of a dam from shore to shore, but only provides for a dam for the South Sault.
A dam to the international boundary.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Perhaps it would foe to the international boundary.
I think the right hon. gentleman is mistaken. The Bill provides for a dam all the way across.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The Bill as introduced in the state of New York provided for a dam from shore to shore, but we will know only when we have the Bill before us. My impression is that the present Bill which has been reported from the committee, and which has taken its first stage at Washington is for the building of a dam across the South Sault.
It also enables them to build from shore to shore. Here is the original Bill which was passed in New York state.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I think my hon. friend is wrong, but we are interested in knowing what would be the effect of the damming of the South Sault, and that alone is quite sufficient to raise a discussion in order to know where we are with reference to it.

Exactly, but this proposition to dam the South Sault is certainly a violation of-the Ashburton treaty If we do not object to the damming of the South Sault we will certainly be allowing them to violate the Ashburton treaty without protest. I do not think that the United States Congress would pass a Bill which violates the Ashburton treaty if we notify them to that effect, and I think the Prime Minister in the name of Canada should enter his objection at once. If the Canadian government is silent our silence may be taken for consent. The Prime Minister knows that prominent Canadian lawyers have been engaged bv this company to appear before Congress and I understand they have represented that this is satisfactory to the Canadian government, so that we should take measures not to leave them under any wrong impression about that.

As reported in the press this company is authorized
To construct, maintain and operate for navigation, water-power and other purposes for 99 years a dam or dams in so much of the St. Lawrence river as lies sonth of the international boundary line between the United States of America and the Dominion of Canada, near Long Sault, Barnhart, and Sheik islands either independently or in connection with like works now erected or to he erected in so much of said river as lies north of said international boundary line, with a bridge or bridges and approaches thereto and a lock or locks, a canal or canals, and other structures appurtenant thereto.

Then, if that be true it is plain that the Prime Minister misunderstands the nature of the Bill before Congress. I shall send a copy of this over to the Prime Minister and I trust a nrotest will be entered by him. I am quite satisfied that the right hon. gentleman is as anxious as I am to protect our great waterway system, and if he has been misled as to the intentions of these people he should at once communicate with the authorities at Washington so as to stop this Bill going through Congress.

I wish to say a few words in connection with this matter, not from any sentimental reason as expressed by the hon. member for South Lanark, but because it anpears to me there is a principle involved in this question which should be settled by the Canadian parliament. I am opposed to the damming of the St. Lawrence river and I believe it to be in the interests of the Canadian people that we should oppose it. Last year we had a discussion extending over several hours on this matter, and it was then stated to the House that certain interests had applied to the government to be permitted to dam the river; that the-"- ..a submitted certain plans, that 'the government sent three engineers to the place to examine the situation, and, that these engineers reported against the project. I understand the idea was to build a dam some 50 feet high so as to create about 600,000 horse-power. Then those interests came back to the government about a year afterwards with amended plans and -the same engineers were sent to report upon the amended scheme and the^ reported it to be satisfactory. What struck me in examining the reports of those engineers i=- that they looked at the matter purely from the standpoint of the feasibility of erecting a dam and creating that quantity of horsepower without doing damage to the immediate neighbourhood, but, what I should like to have seen brought out by the engineers was the economic value of the project to the people of Canada. That point was not touched upon as it should be. I do hope that our engineers when acting for the people of Canada would in dealing with such questions take into consideration the economic side of the question. The question arises: Do we need the development of 300,000 horse-power on the St. Lawrence near the city of Montreal. I sav we do not. I believe there is sufficient water-power in ilie immediate neighbourhood of this city to supply the needs of the people of eastern Canada for many years to come. If we had a proper inventory of our water-powers and if wre had any authority who could tell us the needs of this country at the end of the next 100 years, and should it be discovered that we have sufficient power for our 921
own purposes and some to spare, I would be willing to join in obliging our neighbours. But, when we have private interests coming here asking for the right to dam the St. Lawrence river, insistent applicants who will return year after year, it is high time for the government to lay down the policy that the St. Lawrence river is not to be touched so far as the Canadian side is concerned. I should like to hear the government announce that they will not join in any movement to dam that great waterway from the American to the Canadian side. The St. Lawrence river is one of the scenic routes of the world; its scenery to-day is one of the assets of the country, and it will become a more valuable asset as time rolls on. The scenic beauty of the St. Lawrence is now a valuable asset to the cities of Montreal, Quebec, and Toronto, and we should not lose sight of the fact that apparently it is of no corresponding value to cities on the other side of the line. However, that may be, I have never yet heard it stated that the people of Canada need the power which it is proposed to secure by damming the St. Lawrence river at this place. Last year the Minister of Public Works announced that if the river should be dammed he would see that Canada received one-half the power. I go further than the minister; I do not lose sight of the fact that we have 7,000,000 people in Canada as compared with 90,000,000 in the United States, and my doctrine is:	Equal division yielding
equal benefits. That is the doctrine we should insist upon, and so far, as I am concerned, if these very persistent private interests have got the. government committed in any way to the damming of the St. Lawrence; then, we should take care that for everv 500 horse-power taken out on the American side the same amount should be taken out in Canada and put to beneficial uses here. That is the doctrine I believe in.
I submit, however, in the interest of the country that the St. Lawrence river should be left alone so far as Canada is concerned.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I speak with a good deal of hesitation on this question as I cannot attempt to deal with anything that has been said on either side to-day, but I have followed with the closest possible attention everything which, up to the present time, has been said in this House either last year or this year referring to this matter. It is inevitable, I suppose that I should look at this subject very largely from the lawyer's standpoint, but while I know that is so, I am consoled by the reflection that it is very seldom indeed that good law is not good sense; and' in whatever I have to say in the matter, I hope hon. gentlemen will do me the justice to believe that I am not trying to lay down the law at all, tout that I wrnnt merely such

viaws as I have on the subject to be treated by my fellow members just according to the amount of sense that they think there is behind them. The question here properly concerns our international relations with the United States, and in that sense is one, I take it, of international law.^ But while we use the phrase ' international law,' understanding very well what we mean by it, I think we ought always to remember that, after all, there is no one competent to say with any authority, what international law is, or what it requires. There are no statutes, no enactments of parliament, defining what is the law of nations; there is no court, no judge, who can authoritatively declare this or that or the other principle to be one which nations must regard; and we are driven, in endeavouring to see what are the rights of peoples as a matter of international law, back to the relations which exist between individuals in the same community and governed by the same law. Now, if you think of the situation of this river, apart from any international agreements, but simply as a matter of what this country could do about it if the United States saw fit to place any obstruction in a channel of the river which is wholly within their territory, I think it is manifest that we should be practically helpless, exactly as, if the facts were reversed and Canada were proposing to erect any dam or obstruction in a channel of the river which was wholly Canadian, the United States would be practically helpless to prevent it. The most that could be done by either nation would he in the way of expostulation to the other -representations that you ought not to do this, that it is not fair or right that you should. As a matter of fact, we have international agreements to which we can refer and appeal, if we can satisfy either ourselves or our neighbours that any transgression of these agreements is being contemplated. But in the absence of such agreements, there would be no security even to what we regard as the paramount right of navigation, much less any means practically existing by which, if a proposed work in the United States were going to damage property in Canada, or a proposed work in Canada were going to damage property in the United States, the country which feared the damage, could prevent that damage being done. But it is always founded upon the circumstance that the.Te will be damage. Suppose this stream were all in one country; suppose that the International boundary had been fixed on the 44th parallel instead of the 45th, so that all the territory in question would be in Canada; and, to avoid *any complication, let us assume it all to" lie in the one province of Ontario. Now, what would be the right Sir ALLEN AYLESWORTH.
even in law or in equity, of a man who owned property on the north shore of the river as against the people on the south shore, who might be wanting to do the very thing which is proposed to he done in this instance? That right would simply be-in the sense of the thing surely-would be that if the .proposed work were going to damage the man on the north shore, the courts would stop it. He has a right to have the Tiatural level of the water preserved as it passes his land. If he is going to be flooded by the proposed work, or if the level is going to be lowered to his damage, he can prevent it if he goes to the court and takes proper steps to do so. So that at the basis of the whole right, in honesty or sense, to make any objection, there lies the hypothesis that damage is going to be done, that the level of the water is going to be changed to some man's detriment. And that is equally the basis of any reasonable ground of expostulation by one country to another, if conditions exist such as are said to be found in this case. If it is reasonably manifest that the effect of putting this proposed obstruction in the United States channel of the St. Lawrence at the Long Sault will raise the level or lower the level on the Canadian side, to the detriment of Canadian property owners, there is a reasonable ground for expostulation; and, happily in this instance, by reason of treaty arrangements, there is more than that. There is a basis upon which objection can be taken on our part that would certainly be effective. But unless there is plainly going to be such damage, there is no ground to object. Nobody is hurt, and there would be no foundation for an objection or expostulation, if we made it.
Now, let me ask hon. gentlemen to think of the situation on the ground at this place. We all know more or less about it, from our general knowledge of the geography of the country. I happen to have the advantage of personal knowledge by having been all over Sheik's island on foot and having examined this very locality. We have the main channel of the St. Lawrence and two islands in the channel-Sheik's island, wholly Canadian, the Long Sault island, wholly in the United States; the boun- * dary running in the main channel between the two islands; the United States island up-stream, but the two islands overlapping each other, for a considerable portion of their length, a channel between the United States island and the mainland of New York state, and a channel, when things were in a state of nature, between the north side of Sheik's island and the mainland of the county of Stormont. Canada has interfered with the natural condition of things at this point. lit has not left the natural channel between Sheik's island

and the mainland of Ontario open, as it was in a state of nature. Canada, for its own purposes, has had a dam built at the upper end_ of Sheik's island, which prevents the inflow into the natural channel of any water from the Long Sault rapids. Canada has appropriated that natural channel between Sheik's island and the mainland of Ontario as a part of its Cornwall canal for the purposes of navigation and incidentally for the creating of waterpower, because at the lower end of Sheik's island is another dam and the surplus water forms a mill-pond which is used for the purpose of creating power. I have never heard that Canada consulted the United States before interfering in that way with the natural condition of things at that point. Any one in Canada would have said to such a proposition: What have the United States to do about it? We are not proposing to alter the level on their side, we are not going to do them any harm, we are simply utilizing our own property, and we think we can make better use of it than by leaving it in its natural state.
Have we any more right to protest or expostulate with the United States if they propose to use the channel on their side for their own purposes and in the manner which to them may seem best? I cannot see how, either as a matter of international law, or private law, or reason, or common sense we could do so. Some company, I understand, proposes to build a dam at the foot of the channel on the American side between their island and their mainland in New York state. What is going to be the effect? Of course it will interfere with navigation at once unless, as I understand is intended by the scheme, the interests of navigation are to be protected by the construction in the dam of a lock, making the dam in that way not an impediment, but actually an advantage to navigation. The effect then will be to create a mill pond above the dam between the United States island and the main shore of New York state. If the dam is not constructed so high that it will back the water around the upper end of the United States island, but will still, notwithstanding its presence at the foot of that channel, leave the level in the mill pond not as high as the water at the head of the island, it is surely manifest there can be no effect on the level on the Canadian side. I fully concede that the moment a dam at the foot of this island is made higher than the level of water at the head of the island, it will flood the channel and interfere with the level on the Canadian side. There would be ground for expostulation, for more than expostulation, under existing treaties, if that dam were built high enough to raise the level higher than the upper end of the United States island and thus
affect the level on the Canadian side. But are we to assume that this dam will be of such a height? I cannot assume it. On what ground would we have the right to do so? The interest of the parties desiring to build the dam, according to their statement, can he perfectly well served by the building of a dam which is not high enough to back the water around the upper end of the island, and if they are limited by their charter to the construction of a dam which will not back the water above the head of the island, they cannot affect the Canadian shore, and .the interests of navigation are the only things to be considered.
That is exactly the situation under the existing treaties. The right of navigation is paramount and that right is secured. That right exists in this United States channel which it is proposed to dam, just as it exists in the old channel between Sheik's island and the mainland of Ontario which is to-day utilized as part of our Cornwall canal. The right of navigation is secured by treaty and is not proposed to be interfered with. On the contrary, it is proposed to be helped according to the plans of the promoters, and unless the right of navigation is interfered with, or the level altered on our_own side, we have, under existing treaties, no cause to obj ect.
I do not think much is to be gained by going back to the terms of the Ashburton treaty because we have a new treaty on this very subject which goes further, which governs this very situation, and which has been ratified by both countries and is in force to-day. Under the provisions of that treaty while it prohibits the construction of any obstructions in boundary waters except under certain circumstances, it impliedly gives permission to obstruct boundary waters. The provision of article three of the new Waterways treaty is to the effect that ip addition to existing obstructions, no further obstructions, whether temporary or permanent, of boundary waters on either side of the line-and the whole river is a boundary water from main shore to main shore-no new obstruction on either side affecting the natural level or flow of the boundary waters on the other side of the line shall be made except by the authority of the United States or the Dominion of Canada, within their respective jurisdictions and with the approval of the International Joint Commission. Now the wording of that exception plainly implies that each country, within its own jurisdiction, has the right to authorize obstructions in waters such as these. No new obstructions, it says, shall be made affecting the natural level on the other side of the line except by the authority of the United States or

the Dominion within their respective jurisdictions.

Does my hon. friend think that that provision which deals with the question of the height of water only, supersedes article seven of the Ashburton treaty? Does that provision, just read, supersede article, seven of the Ashburton treaty? It does not seem to me that they refer to exactly the same thing.
What is article 7?
The article my hon. friend has read, which provides that the channels of the St. Lawrence shall be equally free to the ships, boats and vessels of both parties.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I have no doubt that, whatever I say, I shall see tomorrow that I have not dealt, as I should like to deal, with what has been said by the hon. gentleman (Mr. Lennox). But, dealing with it as far as I am able to do at the moment, I would by no means say that the provisions of the recent Waterways treaty supersede those of the Ashburton treaty. Surely both can well stand together, the Ashburton treaty securing equal freedom for purposes of navigation- that is, freedom equally to the inhabitants of one country and those of the other country-in the river which constitutes the boundary, and the recent treaty providing that no new obstruction shall be put anywhere along that river on either side of the line which will have the effect of raising the level on the other side of the line, except: First, with the authority of the government of the country in which the obstruction is to be placed, and, second, with the approval of the International Joint Commission. Now, that language, I say, implies that the government of each country has the right to authorize, if it sees fit, such an obstruction as will alter the level on the other side of the line, and that obstruction, when it has been authorized by the proper government, must also receive the approval of the International Joint Commission before it can be permitted- the two things must concur. The language implies that there is a right, without any infraction of treaty obligations, on the part of either Canada or the United States, to authcrize such obstruction as may affect the level on the other side of the boundary if, in the judgment of the legislature of Canada or the United States, such obstruction is desirable. Now, we have a proposition in the Congress of the United States to authorize such an obstruction. It is entirely within their legal right; they are not infringing upon any treaty obligation by entertaining that proposition. But, if they see fit to authorize it, then, if it will affect Sir ALLEN AYLESWORTH.
the level on the Canadian side of the boundary, it must receive the approval of the International Joint Commission before it can be permitted. That is an additional safeguard which we have secured by entering into this recent treaty. But, without it, if we had no treaty at all, we should simply be in a position where, without anything to rely upon except the natural sense of justice which should be common to all people, we were seeking to protest or expostulate with the United States in what they were proposing to do. In the circumstances which exist, Mr. Speaker, I think it would be difficult for us to frame any line of diplomatic objection or remonstrance which would have any effective foundation. It could at once be answered by the United States that, under the terms of our treaty, we have the right to consider the advisability of doing this, and you are perfectly protected by the creation of this International Joint Commission upon which you are equally represented.

The hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff) stated that, under the Act of 1901, we had given the country the right to erect dams and utilize this power. Will the Minister of Justice please say whether he has seen this Act, and whether that statement is correct?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I do not know that I apprehend correctly the point the h<5n. gentleman from South Lanark (Mr. Haggart) has presented. There is a statute of 1901 to incorporate the St. Lawrence Power Co. I have not examined it with any care, but, glancing over it as it has been handed to me, it appears to give power to the company to dam the St. Lawrence river-to what extent I am not able to say upon such cursory examination. I think it would be perfectly competent for the United States Congress on the one part and the Canadian parliament on the other, to authorize ihe construction of a dam in the St. Lawrence, each on its own side of the boundary, and joining at. the boundary, if the two legislatures saw fit to do so. But such a structure would at once be obnoxious to the recent treaty, even if it would not be entirelv opposed to the provisions of the Ashburton treaty, and such a structure could not have, under the recent treaty, the approval of the International Joint Commission, because not only would it be an obstruction to navigation, but it would have the effect of raising the level of the water on both sides of the boundary line.

What I wanted to know was whether this is merely an empowering Act, granting the company the power to build these works if they secured

the right, to do so, or whether it does give them the right to build the works and use the power?

Perhaps the hon. gentleman would allow me to call attention to the provision of the Act'of 1901, which authorizes the erection of certain dams, but provides that before the work shall be commenced the plans must be submitted to and approved by the Governor in Council.

My question goes further than that. Has the country passed over to the company the right to utilize that power, or is this merely an Act enabling the company, when they get that power, to construct these works?
My hon. friend is correct in the latter statement ; it authorizes the company to construct these works, provided they get the necessary approval of their plans by the Governor in Council.

There are two distinct things. One is the conferring of corporate power upon the company to undertake this work, in other words, to declare that the undertaking of this work would be within their corporate powers. My hon. friend from Lanark (Mr. Hag-gart) wants to know whether it is, merely that, or whether it does not further actually invest this company with the authority of the parliament of Canada to do that work in the River St. Lawrence as far south as the boundary line.

I think the latter statement would give the authority of the charter correctly. There is no doubt that parliament authorized the company to construct these works in the St. Lawrence ; but it provided that before they commenced any work they must have the approval of the Governor in Council of their plans. I understand, pursuant to that authority, the company did do certain work between Sheik's island and the mainland. I think I may take this opportunity of recalling to the memory of my hon. friend, ias well as of other hon. gentlemen, that at the last session of parliament, when a Bill was introduced by my hon. friend from West Lambton (Mr. Pardee), a Bill not proposing, as my hon. friend from Halifax seemed to think, to give to the company which vr>as then being incorporated any authority to dam the St. Lawrence, but merely creating a power transmission company, there was some anxiety upon the part of hon. members of this House with reference to the works, which the company incorporated some nine or ten years ago was authorized to carry on. The Prime Minister then gave the assurance to parliament that the government would not approve of any plans for further
obstructing the St. Lawrence until the whole matter had first been submitted to parliament, and until the approval of parliament had been obtained. And further, a little later, when the Bill was under consideration, I myself drew an amendment ; I am not sure whether it was moved by the hon. gentleman who had charge of the Bill or not ; tout at all events, it was moved and carried, and forms a part of the statute, and it is in these words:
Nothing in this Act shall be deemed to constitute an approval by parliament of any future development of water-power by erecting a dam in or across the St. Lawrence river under the chapter 111 of the statutes of 1901, intituled ' An Act to incorporate the St. Lawrence Power Company,' or otherwise; nor shall the company hereby incorporated be authorized to transmit power generated by the St. Lawrence Power Company other than the power generated by and in connection with the works already constructed by the said St. Lawrence Power Company.
There is a further provision contained in section 12, as if the assurance of the Prime Minister and the section which I have just read were not sufficient, and that further provision sets forth :
The Governor in Council shall not give his approval to the construction of any further canals, water courses, raceways, dams, wing dams, sluices or other works on the River St. Lawrence by the St. Lawrence Powder Company, under the provisions of chapter 111 of the statutes of 1901, or otherwise, nor agree to or approve of any terms or conditions respecting the diversion of water or power from Canada, the consideration and rate to be paid therefor, the location of all dams and generating plant, the reservation of power for use in Canada, the safeguarding of Canadian canals, adjacent lands and navigation, the procuring of consent thereto from the British government under the Ashburton treaty or any other treaty, unless and until the plans, specifications and all terms and conditions shall have been first submitted to and approved by parliament.
I think it is, therefore, abundantly clear, both from the assurance of the Prime Minister as to what will be the action of the government, and also by the terms of these two sections which I have read, that no approval of any works upon the Canadian side of the St. Lawrence would toe given, or could be given, until the matter had first been submitted to, and approved by .parliament. Now, I desire, Mr. Speaker, just to add a few words in reference to the observation of the leader of the opposition with regard to the Bill which was introduced at the last session, and which I have now in my hands. The hon. gentleman stated that the design of that Bill was to authorize the company to erect a dam across the St. Lawrence river. From my seat I ventured to deny that, and the hon. genfle-, man, departing from that courtesy one

would expect from a gentleman who, I think, is desirous of always being considered courteous, the hon. gentleman said it was contradicting him, as I was in the habit of contradicting, without reason and without knowledge of the facts. I desire, Mr. Speaker, to say that outside of this House certain newspapers, and certain gentlemen have sought wrongfully, most improperly, and I say wilfully, and with a view to injure certain persons to convey the impression that the design of this Bill, as introduced by my hon. friend from West Lambton, that the design of myself, and of certain other members of this House who supported that Bill, was to authorize the damming of the St. Lawrence. I say that you cannot find from beginning to end of that Bill as it was first introduced, any provision, any clause, any word, which would give authority to dam the River 'St. Lawrence, i desire to make this public statement, and to assert now- this is perhaps the first opportunity I have had during this session-that a gross wrong has been attempted in certain newspapers of this country in seeking to create the impression that the Bill as first introduced at the last session of parliament, had as its object to grant authority to dam the St. Lawrence river. I say it was, at the beginning when it was first introduced, it was during all its stages while passing through this House, it was when finally passed out of this House with the amendment, it was simply a Bill authorizing the transmission of electricity. When passed through the House it was neither less nor more than that, simply a Bill authorizing the transmission of electrical power. And, Sir, it is a curious fact that my hon. friend the Minister of Railways, in speaking on this Bill last session, referred to a water-power which either had been developed or was being developed at Waddington, upon the American side of the St. Lawrence, and said that if power could not foe obtained from any other source that power might be utilized for the distribution of electricity to the various points of eastern Ontario where people were very anxious to set electrical energy, and, that in certain remarks which were made by Mr. Beck, of the Ontario government, a leading member of the Hydro-Electric Commission, he was reported to have made the statement that the commission were at that very moment negotiating for obtaining water-power from a plant generating electricity at Waddington, upon the United States side of the St. Lawrence, they were in negotiation with the owners of that power for the purpose of obtaining electrical energy, to bring it across tire St. Lawrence, and to transmit it to various sections in the province of Ontario. I felt, Mr. Speaker, that in justice to myself, and in justice to the gentlemen who supported Mr. PUGSLEY.
the Bill which was introduced by my hon. friend from West Lambton, I shohld take an opportunity of referring to misstatements which had been made outside this House, and of correcting the error which my hon. friend the leader of the opposition, forgetting, as he must have forgotten, the contents of the Bill as introduced, fell into with regard to the provisions of the Bill as first introduced last session.
The statement I made was absolutely and entirely correct, and I will take a later opportunity of showing that it was so.

This is a question which affects the people that I represent directly, perhaps as much as any people in the province. I think I know .the local conditions surrounding this question as well, if not better, than any man in the House, outside of the hon. member for Stormont county (Mr. Smith), this region having been my stamping ground as a young man, and I have been on these islands, the Long Sault, North Sault, South Sault, the waters contiguous to them and the land as well. As to the question which came up in the House last session, I was very anxious to have a Bill passed authorizing the construction of a transmission line. I then thought that I would be able, and I am in hopes yet that I will be able, to get power for the town of Brockville and the surrounding districts by a transmission line of some sort. I said then, and I repeat now, that I expected to get it independently of any new development at the Long Sault. There are two powers, as my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugsley), has said, in the same condition, except that one is capable of much greater development than the other, on the St. Lawrence. One is at Waddington, opposite the village of Morrisburg in the county of Dundas. The main river Tuns to the head of Ogdenls island about three and three-quarters miles west of Morrisburg. Then it divides at the head of Rapide Plats. The main channel goes on the north side of Odgen's island ; what is known as Little river, goes on the south side between Ogden's island and the state of New York, or the town of Waddington. Many years ago authority was given in the state of New York to construct a dam there, and it was constructed without any reference to Canada, as I understand, it being altogether in United States territory and the entire stream of Little river being contiguous to the state of New York. For some years that water-power was used and then allowed to go into disuse on account of lack of transportation facilities by rail largely, the dam has been destroyed, or nearly so, and there is really no water-power to-day. It is undeveloped and any person who pro-

poses to supply power from Waddington, must remember that there is no power there to supply until it is developed by somebody with cash coming from somewhere. Now, we go down the river and we find Long Sault island. At what is known as Dickinson's Landing, or in the vicinity of it, the main channel of the Sault goes to the north and, just as in the case of Ogden's island, this island separates the St. Lawrence into the North Sault and the South Sault. The North Sault is the main channel. Hon. gentlemen forget, in discussing this question that no steamer goes down through the North Sault or the South Sault carrying any appreciable amount of freight. Large steamers use neither channel. They have to take the Canadian canal, so that, any interference with either of these channels -would not interfere one iota in so far as navigation is concerned, with the carrying a large amount of the products of the west to the east, as these products, in the large vessels, have to go through the Canadian canal. Now, we find the South Sault all in American territory. At that particular point at least seventy per cent of the North Sault is altogether in United States territory as well. We perhaps forget in discussing it, that while we have a joint share in it we must not presume at all that at this particular point Canada owns the St. Lawrence river as most of it is in the United States, especially at the point where they propose to construct this dam. All of the South Sault is in the United States just as the Little river is in the United States at Waddington. Opposite Waddington on the Canadian side we have constructed a canal running from the head of Rapide Plats to the village of Morrisburg without the consent of anybody and the government are supplying water-power from the St. Lawrence river to several industries in the village of Morrisburg and also power for the running of the waterworks at Morrisburg. When we get to Cornwall we find the same condition. Those who have not lived along the St. Lawrence cannot have the same feeling. But I have not been able to bring myself to the point where I would care to see a dam stretching across the St. Lawrence from shore to shore at the Long Sault. It strikes me as something in regard to which I would need a lot of convincing before I would consent. I want hon. gentlemen to hear that in mind because I have been criticised for the attitude that I have taken. I took this attitude, thinking that I would be able to help the people I represent to get something that they are very anxious to possess. I have said that the interests of navigation must be kept paramount. No matter what else happens the great navigation and transportation interests of the Dominion must be the first
thing that the people of Canada must look to and any power that may be developed, must be subsidiary to the greater interest of transportation. Now, Sir, having that in view, I come down to Cornwall. I find that Sheik's island is in something the same position as regards the Canadian shore as Ogden's island is at Waddington. The small stream between Sheik island and the Canadian shore probably was never navigated except by very small craft, but there was a stream running on the Canadian side.

You are labouring under the same error that the hon. Minister of Justice was labouring under. There was a dam across. Mr. Snet-singer owned a mill there, and it was expropriated from him before the Sheik's island dam was constructed.

Mr. Snetainger owned a small mill of some kind and he owned a small dam, but it was expropriated as my hon. friend from Lanark (Mr. Haggart), has said. That bears out what I am saying that the government permitted that to be done by a private company which is even worse than the government doing it themselves.
Was it part of the St. Lawrence ?
Part of the channel of the St. Lawrence.
It was erected before the canal was there at all.

Well, the river was there anyway, and the dam was erected by the consent of some person, showing clearly that it had been always conceded, at Wad-dinigton on the American side where the Little river was dammed by a private company and on the Canadian side at Sheik's island, where a dam was erected by a private company, that in Canadian territory, where no interests of navigation were affected, the United States had no rights and that in the United States, where navigation was not affected, the Canadian government had no rights. That has always been conceded.
The new treaty says that that shall not be done any more.

We have made an improvement in that respect I admit. Now, I come to the Ashburton treaty. Just allow me ito look at the legal side of the question for a moment. One provision of our agreement with the United States is, that our canals shall he as free to the vessels of the United States as they are to our own vessels. That does not mean that we cannot charge both fees if we like. According to the contention of some hon. gentlemen,

we must at all times, allow their vessels to go through our canals free. It does not mean anything of the kind; it says that thev shall be equallv free, and if we see fit to reimpose a fee on vessels going through the Canadian canals, United States vessels could be charged the same fee without any infraction of the agreement with the United States^ The Ashburton treaty says that Canadian vessels on the one side and American vessels on the other shall be equally free to pass up and down.
That was extended by the Washington treaty which made all waters of the United States free to Canadian subjects.

Yes, that is what the Ashburton treaty meant. As I have intimated. I had not any idea directly or indirectly of giving any person the right to dam the North Sault by the Bill that was introduced last year. It was merely to get a transmission line by which power that already exists could be transmitted to some of the towns that need it so very badly. Now, the South Sault is altogether on the American side and, reiterating what I have said about the North Sault, I want to say frankly that if the South Sault, which is altogether in United States territory, can be utilized to produce power for the people along the St. Lawrence and for others, without doing damage to property owners on either side of the river unless thev are fully compensated or, without injuring navigation, I am in favour of acquiescing in the project to make the proposed improvements at the South Sault.
Could we get a guarantee that we would get half of that power?
If we had any right under the law to have it I would insist on getting it.	.
Do we give them half the power of the Cornwall canal?
No, we do not give them any of the Cornwall canal power.

If the power developed were used on the other side of the line I do not see where our advantage would
be.

My position would be this: I believe that we would get a good deal of that power on the Canadian side. I am not sure, because it is a matter of law, what rights we would have, but I certainly would use to the utmost any rights we might have to get for Canada some share of the power developed on even the South Sault. And if that can be done, then instead of giving away some of our natural Mr. GRAHAM.
resources we would be getting the people of the United States, to give us some of theirs. If any scheme would injure property or interfere with navigation, mark you, I would vote first, last and all the time against it.
