But, if it can be done otherwise, then I believe I am working in the interests of the people of the Dominion of Canada, and in the interests of my own constituents, if I could be a party to an arrangement by which it was provided that some of the power developed from the part of the river in the United States should come to Canada. I know the local conditions very'well, I know every foot of the ground, and if as has been said power can be developed on the south side without injuring our interests then, if we could get part of that power it would be to the benefit of Canada, to allow that Bill to go through the United States Congress without any remonstrance from us, even if we haye the right to remonstrate. What I want in my riding is to get power, I don't care from whom or from where if I get it it a reasonable price, and without doing injury to any interest.

What about
the scenery?
I have never been able to convince myself that I would allow the beautiful scenery on the north side to be touched; that is the way I feel about it.
Hear, hear.

I have taken a great deal of interest in the matter, and I thought that perhaps it might interfere with our canals, because mark you we have a ana, on our side and the United States propose to build one on their side. I have a new man on the engineering staff of the department, who is said to be very competent, and two or three months ago I asked him to examine the situation in the vicinity of Waddington and Morrisburg, and also the Little river and the South Sault, and o report to me his candid conviction as to what effect it might have on our canals. I expected to have that report before now, and when. I get it I shall lay it on the table of the House. I do not know what this engineer's opinions are or what his report may be, but whatever it is it will be interesting to the House, and I shall submit it as soon as I get it.

In the English House of Commons whenever an international question is discussed the practice is to forget party, and to think only of the welfare of the country, and I am glad to say that this debate so far has followed that practice. As nearly as a layman can interpret the proposition which the Minister of Justice laid down in a somewhat in-

volved way, it is that every country has the right to do as it pleases in its own territory. In this instance the United States and Canada have under the Ashburton treaty surrendered their sovereign rights to permit neither nation navigating in the territorial waters of each and the same privilege is applied to another part of the international waters below Detroit. So far as the consideration of this question is concerned the maintenance of unobstructed navigation should be paramount for the two countries, but when we examine the navigation routes along the Great Lakes we find that wherever there is a strategic point the United States government has endeavoured to short-cut it, create a deeper channel than we have, and so lead the business to their territory. At the Sault on the St. Mary's river the Americans have short-cut a channel through what is known as Mud or Hay lake, and thus diverted the traffic through their territory. All that traffic of ours from Lake Superior comes down through territory over which they have sovereign rights, and which they can close against us whenever it suits them. We cannot bring a vessel drawing more than twelve feet of water from Lake Superior to Lake Huron unless through their territorial waters. On the Detroit river we find that the American government has seized another strategic point, and they have within the last few years proceeded to dear a very large canal at what they call the Lime Kiln Crossing. They have erected large dams there and they have virtually ruined the navigation of the Detroit river in Canadian waters. There is at the present time before the Canadian government an application-which has not been laid on the table of the House, and which I think we should have laid on the table of the House -asking for the right to dam the Canadian side of the river which would stop navigation entirely on the Canadian side, so that all navigation would be in American waters. I ask the senior minister present if that is not so?
That is not so.
Has not the American government asked this government for permission to dam the waters of the Detroit river at a point called by the sailors Bobalong island?
When I said that it was not so, I understood the hon. gentleman to say that they had asked for authority to completely shut off the navigation on the Canadian side of tlje river.
The hon. gentleman is a beautiful juggler of words.

The hon. gentleman has no right to make such a remark. What they had applied for was authority to
carry a dam from a point in the middle of the stream down to Bois Blanc island.

That is exactly what I said. The hon. Minister of Public Works is an adept at making statements to this House which, while we must accept them in the fullest sense, we must accept with a mental reservation. There is no doubt that they did not apply for power to put in a dam which would totally destroy navigation in Canadian waters.
As the hon. gentleman said they had.

I have no doubt that motor boats and canoes could still go down the river, but so far as large vessels are concerned, the work would entirely destroy the channel. No protest was made by this government against that work, which is a work under the War Department of the United States. The greatest danger to this country lies in this, that that channel is entirely in American waters, and they could close it completely to us at that point, just as they could close the channel in Mud lake. Now, what is that sovereign right of ours at the Long Sault which they are attacking? They are attempting to establish a work which will divert traffic from our canal. They intend to put in a dam and a canal with 20 or 25 feet of water, according to the plans which were laid on the table of this House last session by the Minister of Public Works, which plans showed the damming of the river, although the hon. gentleman denies that to-day. His own words at that date also showed that that was the intention of the company.

I must correct the hon. gentleman. He is making an erroneous statement. He says that I denied that the plans which had been submitted by the company showed a proposal to dam the St. Lawrence river. I never gave any such denial. On the contrary, at the last session of parliament, I stated that the plans submitted by the company did show a proposal to dam the river, but that the government had not approved of those plans.

I am glad that I am getting the hon. gentleman down to earth in this matter. I will bring him further down to earth, and will quote from ' Hansard ' his very words in this House, stating that the intention of the company was to dam the river, although he denies that he said so last session. This is what appears in ' Hansard ':
Mr. Emmerson. Were these plans which were submitted by the St. Lawrence Power

Company to your department for approval, plans for the construction of a work to connect with another work that would come out from the American shore?
Mr. Pugsley. Yes, the plans were for damming the river across from the Canadian side to the American side, and also for the building of a lock for the purpose of improving navigation, the idea being to give an additional lock to the one that is already there, and which was constructed and is owned by the Canadian government.
Will the hon. gentleman permit me?

If the hon. minister will wait till I get through, he can answer all I 'say. When this question of damming the river now comes before this House, the Minister of Justice and the Prime Minister state that the first authority was the Ashburton treaty-that was the primary rule with reference to this channel. The Minister of Eailways and Canals endorsed that. The inference from the involved sentences of the Minister of Justice was that the new treaty was supplementary to the old treaty-that while the old treaty dealt with the right of navigation, the new treaty dealt with the right of developing power, and that anything done either by this parliament or by the Congress of the United States must be approved by the Waterways Commission. I will ask the House if that impression, was not left on the House? But,, strange to say, we had that great constitutional authority, the Minister of Public Works, saying last year something different, in answer to Mr. Sharpe:

Sharpe. What power has the International Waterways Commission to deal with this matter?
Mr. Pugsley. They simply advise.
Now, what protection has this country or the United States from the Waterways Commission in this matter, if we are to accept the word of the hon. Minister of Public Works?

The hon. gentleman is speaking of a different commission altogether. The Minister of Justice referred to the new commission under the treaty which was ratified last session-the International Boundaries Commission.

Then perhaps the Minister of Public Works will tell us what authority the Boundary Commission will have in this matter. Will they have a veto on these plans or on the work if it is authorized by this parliament or by the United States Congress? Now, Sir, with reference to this matter, let us be practical and have a little common sense about it. I always like to hear the Minister of Eailways talk, because he always Mr. CURRIE (Simcoe).
takes a broad view, and it took a good deal of worming and twisting to satisfy his conscience that this work would be in the interest of the public or any one else, except the company that made aluminum. If it is necessary to have that work done to develop power at that point, I think the parliament of Canada and the government of New York state or the United States Congress should cause one of their various commissions to consider the matter seriously, and to see that if the power were developed, the rights of the public would be conserved, and we would not. be turning over to some corporation a valuable franchise which it would immediately proceed to capitalize for $50,000,000 or $60,000,000. If there be anything to be got out of this, if it be necessary to have this water-power developed, let both countries jointly agree upon a plan upon which the development shall take place and decide the quantity of power each country shall have and the price to be paid. The whole trouble is simply this: Every one knows that, an attempt has been made here to rob the public treasury in some way. The whole fight over this question has been due to the fact that a corporation in the United States-one of the most powerful there-which has a monopoly of a certain metal now of very great use in the electrical art, has been endeavouring to seize all the cheap water-powers of both countries for its own use. Let me tell the Minister of Justice that with the increasing use of that metal which that company produces, there will be no hope, should they develop that power, of his having any spare power for Broekville, because the company will use it all for their own purposes in the turning out of aluminum. Would it not be better to keep before the House and country the rights of navigation. The Minister of Public Works has been up to the shoulders fighting' for the company which desires to get this water-power. He has resented the imputation that he has been endeavouring _ to boost this company, and to-day he denied that he ever wished to dam the river or do anything of that kind. Well, I think I could satisfy the House, from his own remarks, that he did, last year, try to have the river dammed, and the company which intended doing this is the same company which is seeking their charter in Washington.

speakeroldname: Mr. C. J. DOHERTY (St. Anne, Montreal).
speechtext:
The announcement made by the right hon. the Prime Minister early in this debate that the government had taken means to communicate with the American authorities with the view of remonstrating against the adoption of the measure now going through Congress, would justify us

in assuming that the government had taken the position that our rights were being infringed upon, or were in danger of being infringed upon by the proposed legislation. But according to the Minister of Justice (Sir Allen Aylesworth) we have no rights in connection with this channel, and no ground upon which to remonstrate or expostulate. That seems to me rather a surprising statement. If the government take the position that even if the channels mentioned in the Ashburton treaty are being closed we have no grounds upon which to remonstrate, I do not think we can expect much advantage from the intervention which the right hon. the Prime Minister told us he was seeking to bring about, through the British ambassador, in this matter now pending before the American Congress. I understand the Minister of Justice to argue that there was1 no need for us to go back to the Ashburton treaty in order to ascertain our rights, because these were to be found in the later boundary water treaty. Subsequently, however, I understood him to say, in answer to a question, that the latter treaty did not supersede the former, and that the provisions of both are to be taken as equally standing. I submit that in order to ascertain what our rights are with regard to these particular channels, we must go to the Ashburton treaty and we will not find them anywhere else. It is perfectly true that after the Ashburton treaty had provided that the channels in the St. Lawrence on both sides of the Long Sault and Barnhart's island shall be equally free and open to the vessels and commerce of both countries, our later treaty provides in a general way that the navigation of the boundary waters shall remain free for the purposes of commerce and navigation to the inhabitants of both countries. But that general provision in the later treaty does not in any way supersede or affect the clear and express provision of the Ashburton treaty with regard to these two particular channels. If I am not greatly mistaken it is an elementary principle in the interpretation of laws and contracts that general dispositions do not derogate from special provisions made to regulate and govern and determine specific eases. I take it, therefore, that notwithstanding the general enactment contained in our last boundary treaty, that treaty does not in any way modify the provision of the Ashburton treaty with regard to these particular channels. In the face of that provision. I must confess that I heard with considerable astonishment the Minister of Justice lav down the principle that we were not concerned in and would have no right to interfere in what was being done on the American side of the river unless there was a question of raising the level of
the water on our side. It is true, he added, that these gentlemen on the other side, who are asking for this power, had declared that they were going to provide in some other way for navigation. They do not deny that these channels, which the treaty says shall be open, are to be barred, but they say they are going to provide for navigation in some other way, and the Minister of Justice, therefore, concludes that we have no ground to expostulate.
Well, in the first place, it seems perfectly clear that what is being done is in violation of the express terms of the treaty. The channels are being barred. I do not suppose that it would be argued that to be equally closed to the people of both countries would mean the same as to be equally open to the people of both countries. I quite agree with the Minister of Railways (Mn. Graham) that the fact that the canals are to be equally free to both parties does not prevent tolls being charged, so long as those tolls do not discriminate against the people of one country. But, on the other hand, I do not suppose that he would carry the argument so far as to conclude that, provided the channels are equally closed to both parties, the provision of the treaty would be complied with.
That loses me in the law.
Would the hon. gentleman mind if I asked him a question? Because, this is a very interesting point.
Certainly not.

Suppose that, on the Canadian side of the St. Lawrence, there were no Cornwall canal. Suppose we said: We are going to improve the navigation, for there are only rapids there with a depth of six or seven feet of water; so we will make a lock and give a depth of twenty feet, and that lock wll be equally open to both countries; would the United States have a right to complain of that? Per contra, suppose the government of the United States says that the South Sault has a depth of only eight or ten feet-my hon. friend the Minister of Railways and 'Canals says it is not so much as that- and they decide to build a lock that will afford a depth of twenty feet and will leave it equally open to both countries; could we complain of that?

Now, with regard to the first question, it seems to me that before there is any occasion to answer that question, one would want to know whether there was a channel, properly speaking on our side. Because that winch is uealt with by the treaty is not, in general terms, the right to navigate the waters anywhere. We have particular channels which are indicated as existing, and it is said that

these channels shall remain open to the ships of both parties. That is not a general declaration that the parties shall be free to navigate in any part. Now, I am willing to take the statement as to the fact of the Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) or the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugsley) as to whether there was any channel on our side which could come within that description. The channels mentioned there, the channels on both sides of Long Sault islands and of Barnhart island, if I understand rightly, are on the American side. The treaty is dealing expressly with channels that are on the American side, actually existing channels, and it provides that they are to be open to us. Now, somebody goes to the American Congress and oays:	We want
leave to close up all these channels, but we will give you something as good. Now-

Pardon me. What the Minister of Justice was referring to particularly was the closing of one channel- not of both-between the ooum Sault and the mainland. That, as I understand it, is not the main channel for navigation purpose.

But I understand that it is one of the channels mentioned. And I am told that the legislation authorizing the making of a dam from the mainland on the American side to the boundary takes in both of these channels mentioned in the treaty.
The Minister of Justice did not deal with that feature.
Yes, he did.
No, he said the channel was between Long Sault island and Barnhart's island.
And also one to the north.

At one stage, if I understood him, he was proceeding to show that the barring was to be done only in the south channel, and argued that unless it was shown that the water -would be dammed back so as to raise the level on The Canadian side, we had no standing ground for remonstrance or expostulation. In other words, here it is publicly and openly proposed to close the channels which, under the treaty, are always to be open to us, and the minister tells us that the matter does not coi,cern us, and we have no standing ground if we desire to remonstrate. The Minister of Public Works ' asks:	Suppose they were going to alter
one of these channels and improve navigation, should we have the interest to object? Certainly we should not have the interest to object,-whatever our right might be- if it were absolutely established that the change was going to improve navigation.

But that is precisely the matter that the Congress of the United States is undertaking to determine. And we are not concerned-I understand the Minister of Justice to say-if the Bill provides that a channel shall be made for navigation.
I was dealing in my question, wholly with the South Sault, which, I understand, is not the main channel and not a good channel.
It is a splendid channel.
Whether good or bad, here is our contract. It deals with the south channel, whatever it may be, and it declares that it shall be equally open to both countries.
Equally free.

I do not think I made a mistake. No, the treaty says ' shall be equally free and open '. If that is not clear, and if it is not clearly applicable to the south channel, then, of course, I do not understand English. But all this is being done ex parte; and when we ask if the government is doing anything about it, we are first given to understand that the government is doing something about it, and this is followed by a statement of the Minister of Justice that, for his part, he does not see that we have any ground to remonstrate or expostulate. And I ask, what good results can we expect from intervention if the government is going into court with a feeling, and that publicly announced, that it has not a leg to stand upon? I do not think the country will gain benefit from the intervention. But, I say that, far from not having ground to stand upon, we have the prima facie ground that our agreement is being violated. It may be true that these gentlemen, or the American government, are in the position to supply something that will be a remedy of the wrong. But it will only be a remedy of the wrong; they first create the wrong by violating the agreement. And I do not understand that, as between parties making an agreement that a thing shall be done in a particular way, it remains open for one to say: I win not do what we agreed to do, but, without consulting you I will do something contrary to our agreement, but I will provide something just as good. At this stage we are vitally interested in having our rights put before the American authorities in the strongest possible way. Mr. Speaker, there has always been, at least for some time, a very great interest manifested in mergers, in concentrations into one company of various industries hitherto operating independently. What is the reason of that interest? In the first place, stock markets, as a rule, are affected by all movements which lead up to the merger of companies, to concentrations which are generally preceded bv variations in the stocks of the companies interested. In the second place, the merging of companies Mr. DOHERTY.

Finally, a merger raises always the important question of whether the commodities produced by the merging industries will either increase or lower in price. In fact, as a general rule, as the House is aware, mergers give rise to a very considerable quantity of speculation, and that is one feature of these mergers which I think it is necessary for the House and the country to he informed about. As a rule, they are productive of very considerable profits to the promoters. How are these profits obtained? Generally by the appropriation, under favourable circumstances, by the promoters of what is called watered stock, or shares in the merging company, resulting from over-capitalization, representing in reality no actual value, but, after the merger, indistinguishable from the rest of the shares and consequently having, it may be, a very considerable market value, though beaind this watered stock there is no actual valre. Thus we have for these twenty companies or so an authorized capital of $214,750,000, of which there has been issued over $168,000,000. This shows the extent of the interest involved; and had I pursued this inquiry further, I have no doubt that I would have been able to extend the list and bring up the capitalization of these special companies to about $300,000,000. Indeed, in an exhaustive and very interesting speech which the hon. Minister of Labour delivered on the 10th of April last, when he moved this House into committee on his Combines Bill, he himself enumerated a considerable number of companies which are not mentioned in this list. So that it is proper, I think, to say that the interest involved in these mergers amounts to hundreds of millions of dollars, and therefore it is very interesting to the public, and particularly to us in this House, to become cognizant of some of the details connected with the organization of such immensely capitalized companies. When an industrial enterprise is in the hands of a firm, and the capital of the firm has been partly lost, it is written off. On the other hand, if the capital is increased, it is because the partners in the firm have left their earnings in the business. The claim of such businesses to special protection, as a rule is, or ought to be, founded on the actual cost of the production of their product. The loss of capital on the part of firms doing business is never admitted to the consideration of parliament when parliament fixes the protective duties. The case of a joint stock company, however, is manifestly a different matter. It is the opening of the capital account which settles the amount on which dividends are expected. As the actual capital in the business goes up or goes down, it does not as a rule bear a relation to the real capital in the business. And the balancing of the books of such companies is in a sense false. By that I mean that the nominal capital of the company as a liability has to be _ balanced by its assets, and these often include the good-will of the business and other fictitious items. Consequently while these companies claim protection upon the cost of production, this cost is



always made to include interest on the capital, though this has sometimes in part been lost or has been issued for good-will, and very often also for tangible considerations and at a very large discount.
Having drawn this distinction between firms entering industrial life, and joint stock companies, let us view for a moment how new enterprises enter into the industrial field. Is it not a fact that, as a rule, on account of the risks involved in a new enterprise, it is often necessary that those who run these risks should get their interest in the enterprise at somewhat less than the nominal value. In some why or other it is arranged to issue stock at a discount. This is frequently done. In some cases there seems some justification for such a proceeding. It may be a proper proceeding on account of the risks involved, or the temporary condition of the money market, and the difficulty of procuring the funds necessary to start the enterprise. There is therefore some justification in the apparent values being in reality greater* than the real material assets of the company at the time of the starting of the enterprise.
The case of mergers of existing enterprises is somewhat different. There can be no objection to a fair conversion into capital of the value of trade-marks and patents, which is often the object of the merging of different companies. But when you come to consider the fixing of a protective or customs tariff, it would seem that we should adopt as a measure the percentage which is necessary to insure the maintenance in activity of only the real actual capital involved in the enterprise and also the maintenance of the labour necessary to carry it on, which has been created by the industry. In fixing that protective or customs tariff, you are surely not to consider in any way the payment of dividends _ or returns upon a fictitious capital which has not been at any time really invested in the business.
Now, what happens at the time of the creation of an industry in our country, and of the willingness on the part of parliament to give it some encouragement by a protective tariff? This happens, that a protection is given slightly in excess of what is absolutely necessary-why? On account of the risks involved in the starting of a new enterprise, in order to induce people to go in, and, instead of provision being made for a gradual reduction of the protective duties necessitated by the starting of the enterprise, the duty is kept up. Then, what happens?
Earnings are considerable; the industry becomes prosperous and generally affords ample dividends. In the face of these earnings, as a rule, competition is provoked But the capital is increased, and so there is a reduction of the rate of dividend from Mr. MONK.
ten or eight to five or four, and it is expected in that way to avoid competitions. Nevertheless, competitors will enter the field if they are aware that conditions are such that with keen attention money may be made. If, in cases of that kind, protection diminished by degrees, this probably would not happen, or else these competitors would, under the necessities of the case, either drop out or diminish their output. But the maintenance of the protective duties tends to increase and intensify the conditions I have described. The next stage is that arrangements are made for fixing prices. But, as you are aware, under legislation passed last session, to do this directly has become difficult if not impossible, and certainly exposes those who enter into such arrangements to prosecution under the law. Other devices are resorted to. You have a common sales agent, which diminishes the expense of placing the products upon the market. Or you have division of districts. But in spite of these methods to protect profits, competition goes on, new competitors crowd into the market; anti then the temptation to merge becomes very great. Mergers in themselves, per se, are not to be condemned. They give good results in many respects. They give to the industries concerned one management; they concentrate; they enable the companies that are brought together to secure the best officers by spending very considerable in that direction _and the best experts to work the industry; they simplify the marketing; they result in many other economies which in themselves are not to be condemned. It is to be noted also that not a single company is exposed to the operation of the law passed last year by this parliament. There can be no charge of combination amongst traders to fix prices where there is only one company. In such cases the operation of that law becomes impossible. And, indeed, I would, at this stage, call this to the attention of the House, that, in these very considerable mergers that have lately taken place, you do not find anything upon which you can base a suit or prosecution under the Act against combines. They have evidently carefully guarded against that. But there would be no necessity for it, since _ a merger is not a combination of companies for the fixing of prices. Now, the necessity or utility of a merger having become apparent, what is the next proceeding? As a rule in these operations-I am speaking of the facts as we learn them from the public prints and from what we hear on the street- those who are engaged in the industries themselves are the first to see in the transactions which will tend to a merger the opportunity for very profitable speculation. Mergers, under the conditions under which they are affected cannot be efficiently carried out without the assistance of institu-

tions that command large capital. It is found necessary in many cases, by the promotors of these mergers, in order to overcome the objections of those who are interested in these different industries who are unwilling to see the combination effected, to operate upon the market and depress the securities of existing companies. It is also necessary, sometimes, in order to overcome opposition for the promoters to win over, with some generosity, those opponents who threaten to impede the evolution of the companies into one company. In spite of these obstacles, there remains still opportunity of very large profit. In what? In the issuing of common stock. Let me give an example illustrative of what I have been describing. Take, for instance, a group of concerns worth, let us assume, exactly $1,000,000, irrespective of protective duties, the existence of which might enhance the value of a concern as their reduction would diminish it. These concerns are in the condition to which I referred a few moments ago. They have been organized; they have lived; competition has come along. But the profits are considerable. They would be capitalized, on the institution of a merger, at, say, $3,000,000; you would have $1,000,000 of bonds secured by mortgage; $1,000,000 of preferred stock, and $1,000,000 of common stock. These securities being provided, how would they be handled? As a general rule-I speak subject to correction by those who know more, perhaps, about these operations than I have been able to learn- to settle with the holders of the existing concerns you would have to provide cash or its equivalent, a first mortgage, bonds, or preferred stock. It is necessary to carry on considerable dealings with the individuals who are holders of the original concern, and with groups in order to get control, for without control it is impossible to finally carry out the merger. It is here that the large financial institutions come in. They underwrite the bonds, we will not say at par, but, in this instance, let us say at 95.
If the bonds are not disposed of otherwise, they are placed with the bank which underwrites them to say at 95. But there are sub-underwriters, men behind who are the promoters, who sub-underwrite the issue at a slight advance over the bank's figures, and it is this slight advance which constitutes the bank's profit. In many instances, the directors of these banks and the directors of the comnanies that are about to be merged, form themselves into a group or syndicate, and it is this syndicate which sub-underwrites the bonds. Common stock is offered to the bank in order to induce it to underwrite the bonds. The bank, therefore, in return for 95 per cent which it pays for the bonds, gets $100 bonds and say 75 per cent of common stock. What be- I 931
comes of these securities? The sub-underwriters take over the bonds and common stock at a slight advance and endeavour to dispose of the bonds and naturally keep as much as possible of the common stock. Then how will the vendors, the original holders, be settled with? How will you provide the working capital? That is provided out of the preference shares which are not wanted for the vendors. Out of the money produced by the bonds you pay the vendors, you pay then with preference shares, and out of what is left you provide working capital. Take the illustrative case just referred to. We will take $250,000 of preference stock for the vendor which will leave $750,000 preference stock for the immediate needs of the new company and which will leave $250,000 of common stock. This common stock is gradually disposed of by the underwriters and mostly by the sub-underwriters. It is hawked about and given as a bonus. Three shares of preference stock and one of common stock are given for $300. Let us look at the result. Out of an issue of securities of $3,000,000 there is realized from the bonds $750,000, from the preference stock $250,000 for the vendor and $750,000 for working capital, and the common stock is given as a bonus for distribution among the promoters. I am not here to offer any opinion upon the moral aspect of a transaction of that kind. Indeed most of those who carry on these operations are looked upon as men of strong moral views in business matters. They are generally philanthropists, interested in good works and are pillars of their churches; but I must say I do not see anvthing particularly wrong in the operation if you leave out of consideration the duties that must be kept up. I see no particular harm except that it results in a number of people acquiring, under the auspices of powerful institutions that lend their aid to these transactions, securities behind which therg is no real value. From the point of view of public interest, which is the one I desire to urge here, there are two serious objections. One of the results of this system of carrying on a business is the creation at on.ce of a strong interest for the maintenance of duties in such a way that dividends will be insured upon all this watered stock which represents in reality no real value. There is a strong interest created among people of powerful influence to see that the duties should not be reduced to the absolute real value and need of those industries, but to keep them at such a figure as will insure dividends being paid upon merely apparent values. Another public interest is this? Our banks, which are engaged in these large operations, are obliged necessarily to tie un a considerable share of their funds. Why? In order to furnish these advances which are always large, and is it not apparent that they ne-

the government and the public would know what amount of the bank's capital has gone into these special merger operations. As I view it, these operations are not in harmony with the operations generally contemplated for banks. Banks that are forbidden by the banking law to loan or advance on mortgages, by the interposition _ of trust companies that hold these bonds, in reality make advances which are secured by a mortgage, an operation which is forbidden by their charter. It is a singular thing that money has (been easy in all the countries of the world this year, but in Canada the market has been tight. Has this been caused by the amount of capital involved in these operations ? Some people who know, are inclined to think so. Money has been tighter here than elsewhere.
Mr. Speaker, I apologize to the House for the time I have taken in exposing this matter, which I consider very important. From words which have fallen from my right hon. friend the Prime Minister upon another occasion, one would suppose that a motion of this kind is a want of confidence motion. But surely that interpretation, with all respect, is not a proper one. The term ' want of confidence motion ' is not properly applicable to a motion made on going into committee of supply; that is to say, it does not apply, in my estimation, more to such a motion than to any other motion. Want of confidence attaches to any motion the result of which is to prove' that the government has lost the confidence of the House. It may occur on a private Bill, it may occur on any government measure, it may occur on a motion apparently indifferent, but the result of which is to express to the government that the House has no more confidence in them. It may result without the expression of any vote at all. Motions made at this stage of the- proceedings are always made for a redress of grievances, and it is quite open to the government either to accept these motions and to redress the grievance, or to express its own opinion that a grievance has been made out, and that it will entertain the demand without their (being such fatal results attached to the motion. Upon one occasion in England, if my memory serves me right, Mr. Gladstone,, when Prime Minister, resigned upon an insignificant vote in Supply, where the committee refused to gTant a small sum of two hundred pounds in the army estimates. Why ? Because Mr. Gladstone considered that it was, on the part of the House, an expression of -want of confidence in the army reforms which his government had undertaken. In 1896 the government of that day resigned without the House meeting. I insist upon this, because I did not present the motion as a motion of want of confidence. I present it at the proper time
for the redress of grievances before we go into Supply, and I would 'be very glad if the government, in view of the importance of the matter, would state its willingness to entertain the proposal and to make thg investigation which is called for by a large number of people-not perhaps influential and powerful people, but people who have been affected by these operations and who think that an investigation is necessary. Upon that assurance from the government I would willingly withdraw the motion. I insist upon this, because I do not wish to be reproached with having presented this motion at this stage, taking the view of our parliamentary practice which I do.

Mr. Speaker, before attempting to reply to my hon. friend (Mr. Monk) I would like" to ask him just what form of investigation he has' in mind when he speaks ot the desirability of the _ subject of recent mergers being publicly inquired into.
It seems to me that a Royal Commission composed of competent men would be the proper way to make a public investigation.

In proposing to the House the appointment of a Royal Commission, or the appointment of any body, to conduct an investigation into such a large question as that of" mergers, it is rather important that the reasons which are given in support of a suggestion of this kind should be made apparent. I have carefully listened to my hon. friend during the course of his remarks and it seems to me that he has succeeded admirably in disclosing to the House the intricate and complicated methods by which mergers are brought into being, by which they are financed and by which their operations are carried on. But the admirable speech which the hon. gentleman has made, it appears to me, has given us the best of reasons why it is not necessary to hold a public inquiry in order to disclose these complicated methods. He has taken one of the most difficult of modern problems and he has shown, I think clearly to everybody, that it is a many sided question and that there are many considerations which have to_ be taken into account in dealing with a subject of that kind. He has done this so well that I think his own speech is sufficient to obviate the necessity of conducting an inquiry to discover these methods and to ascertain the possible effects upon all concerned. However, in the motion which has been put forward the hon. member has given three reasons in particular why he thinks a public investigation of this kind should take place. He suggests that it should take place, first, in order that the government or the country may ascertain to what extent these mergers are responsible for causing continuing high prices for the commodities

produced; second, to what extent they are responsible for damaging the reputation of Canadian securities abroad and, third, restricting the banking facilities of this country. In asking the government to appoint a royal commission of this kind it seems to me that the hon. member should have presented some grounds on which the House would have reason for believing that to some extent mergers had been responsible for injuring the reputation of Canadian securities abroad, for restricting the banking facilities of the country and for the continuation of high prices. While he has spoken at length with regard to the methods of the organization of these mergers, I fail to gather from his remarks anything in the way of what one would regard as prima facie grounds affording justification for a public inquiry. As a matter of fact, Mr. Speaker, I do not think that during the course of his remarks my hon. friend made a single reference to the reputation of Canadian securities abroad. I may have failed to hear all he said, but I followed him very closely and a perusal of his remarks in ' Hansard ' to-morrow will show whether I am right in that or not, but I did not hear a single reference to the reputation of Canadian securities abroad, and yet, that is one of the grounds which he gives why the government should appoint a royal commission to inquire into the effect of mergers in this particular. But, although my hon. friend has not put forward any reason in support of this clause in his motion I cannot help feeling that he has not done so because of the difficulty he would have had in making'out a case in that connection. I think my hon. friend will be the first to admit that there never was a time in the history of the Dominion when Canadian securities stood so well or so high as at the present time. If the existence of mergers is one of the factors entering into the reputation of Canadian securities abroad then, judging by the position at the present time, we would be led to conclude that mergers were a good thing rather than a harmful thing in that particular. One of the most prominent of modern financiers is Sir Edgar Speyer. He will, I think, be acknowledged in this House as being one of the foremost financiers in the British Empire. Giving to one of the leading papers of this country an estimate at the close of last year of the financial situation, Sir Edgar Speyer used the following words:	,
Just as Canada suffered in the nineties through no fault of her own, in common with the rest of the world, through the series of economic misfortunes which affected so many countries at that time, so the good credit which the ivorld at large now enjoys is shared by Canada in an exceptional degree. It is, indeed, of vital importance to Canada to know that the condition of credit generally has
been rarely higher than it is to-day, and that Great Britain may be expected to lend freely in 1911. The indications are that trade will be more active than it has been ever before, and that Great Britain will continue to supply capital to Canada with a generous hand for the development of the great natural resources with which she is endowed so abundantly.
So, we have the testimony of this leading financial expert in London to the effect that during the past year, during the time when these recent mergers have been formed, the credit of Canada stood higher in Britain than it has ever stood before. And yet the hon. gentleman suggests that because of the alleged damage done to Canadian securities by mergers, this House should appoint a -royal commission of inquiry.
I did not allege such damage ; I asked for a commission to ascertain how far these mergers might have an effect upon the reputation of our securities.

In answer to that I might quote the very words of the motion given notice of by the ihon. gentleman :
That the recent mergers of heretofore competing industries and the issue of securities resulting therefrom should be the subject of public investigation, with a view. of ascertaining how far such mergers or the methods of carrying them out affect the public interest, either as causing continuing high prices for the commodities produced, as damaging the reputation of Canadian securities abroad.
I would submit that neither the remarks of the hon. gentleman or the situation as it is known to be in the financial world, afford a reason why on this ground at least the government should appoint a royal commission. My hon. friend further suggests that a commission should be appointed to inquire into the effect of these mergers as restricting the banking facilities of the country. Again, I fail to find that my hon. friend was able to show that the banking facilities of our country had been restricted in consequence of mergers. He did say that it was possible that because of these large financial transactions the banks would possibly be prevented from loaning money in other directions, but such evidence as there is does not appear to support his contention. At the close of the last commercial year loans were made by the banks in Canada amounting to approximately $677,617,000 which was almost $20,000,000 more than the commercial loams by the banks a year previously. During the same time the -banking capital increased by about $14,000,000 as an indication of greater activity in trade, and it may ibe remarked that in that period when the greatest volume of business was being done, namely, the month of September, the note circulation of the banks was *99.400 -

000. So, in the case of banking facilities as in the case of securities abroad, my hon. friend has failed to give any evidence to this House in support of his motion for a royal commission of inquiry. Far from finding any restricting of banking facilities we have the strongest evidence of the greatest expansion yet known in the banking history of Canada,
The last reason given by my hon. friend for the appointment of this commission is that the commission should inquire into the effect of the mergers in causing or continuing high prices for commodities produced. That brings us to the question of prices. If the hon. gentleman would refer to a resolution passed in this House last session he will find there almost the very words he has put into his motion. On the 12th of April last ye;ar this resolution was adopted by the House :
'Resolved, that it is expedient, in connection with Bill (No. 101) now before this House respecting the investigation of combines, monopolies, trusts and mergers, which may enhance prices or restrict competition to the detriment of consumers, to provide for the appointment of Boards of Investigation for the purpose of inquiring into alleged combines causing enhanced prices or restricted competition, for the appointment of counsel to conduct investigations before such boards, and for the payment of the members of such boards and of counsel, and of witnesses appearing before the boards, and of all expenses of boards, including transportation expenses incurred by the members thereof, or by persons under orders of such boards, in making investigations under the Act, and salaries of employees and agents and the payment of clerical and other assistance.
Does the Minister of Labour find that that resolution would authorize the carrying on of such an investigation?

Certainly, and what I want to point out at the moment is that to the extent to which my hon. friend asks this government to appoint a commission to ascertain the effect of mergers on prices, the very object aimed at (by him was obtained by parliament last year, and on the strength of the resolution then passed, was founded legislation which now exists. Let us see for a moment ho,w the legislation of last year is likely as respects effectiveness to compare with what is now suggested by my hon. friend (Mr. Monk). His motion comes down to a request that the government should appoint a royal commission to investigate these various mergers in order to ascertain their effect upon prices. In 1897 the Minister of Finance introduced a Bill giving the government power to conduct an inquiry where there was reason to believe a combine existed for the purpose of enhancing prices, and, notwithstanding that the government were willing to concede that such' an investigation should take place be-Mr. KING.
fore a judge, hon, gentlemen opposite entered the strongest objection against it. They claimed that to put in the hands of the government the power to appoint men te investigate any merger or combine was j to give the Governor in Council a power that was well nigh inquisitorial, that would enable them to harass individual concerns, and for political or other purposes to promote their own ends. I imagine that if my hon. friend (Mr. Monk) were to press his motion he would meet to-night amongst his political friends precisely the same objections as were then advanced by them. For example, the hon. member for East Grey as reported in ' Hansard ' said :
It puts in the hands of -a few, men the power to harrass or annoy or interfere with the operations of business men in the country ... to put the traders and manufacturers of the country under the control of the government to such an extent _ as to keep them in perpetual dread of being attacked under this law. It might be used as a means of levying on .men political contributions or blackmail to any possible extent.
That is the view of one of my_ hon. friend's best friends on the other side of the House, and when my hon. friend's suggestion is met with that kind of argument on his own side of the House, he can expect but slight support for his motion.
Now, I differ with my hon. friend altogether when he says that the existing legislation is not sufficient for the purpose he has in view. I doubt if it is possible for more effective legislation to be devised than that on the statute-book at the present time, known as the Combines Investigation Act. Who knows better than the consumer whether or not he is being affected adversely by a combination? Who under my hon. friend's proposal is to be the judge as to what industries are to be singled out for investigation? Does he propose that this royal commission shall^ investigate every merger in the Dominion? If he does, the work of that commission is going to be very large and extensive. If he does not, who is to determine which merger is to be the subject of investigation in the first instance? Under the legislation on the statute-book, if any body of consumers have reason to believe that trade is being to some degree restricted by a combination, they have power, if they can make out a prima facie case, to secure an investigation; they have also power to put on the board of investigation one of their own number; and, in order that the investigation may be carried out in as fair a manner as possible, opportunity is given to the other side, namely, to those interested in the merger, also to name a member of the board. These two, agreeing together if they can, upon a judge, name him as chairman. They failing to agree, it is left to the government to appoint the third;

and these three gentlemen are given all the powers of a court-the power to compel the production of documents, the power to summon witnesses, the power to take evidence under oath. In other words, all the powers a royal commission can possibly have, are given by the legislation we already have, to deal with this very question which my hon. friend suggests should be dealt with by a royal commission. So I say there does not appear to be any reason for appointing this commission on the grounds he has named in his motion, while legislation which is more effective than what he proposes already exists, and exists in a form which is likely to be of greater service to those who are being adversely affected by any of these alleged combinations.
My hon. friend and some of his friends on tlie other side may say: we know of the existence of these mergers, but what investigations have taken place? And I suppose that because there have been no investigations under that law up to the present time, they will say that the law lias been ineffective. If my hon. friend has that thought in his mind, I ivould ask him how he tests the effectiveness of other legislation. To take a very obvious case, we do not estimate the effect of the death penalty by the number of death sentences passed or the number of hangings in a year. If the number is few, we believe the legislation is effective. If there are none we regard it as a most effective deterrent. The strength of lifesaving apparatus is not measured by the number of drownings that take place, but rather by the lack of number. So it is with legislation of this sort. The knowledge that the power exists on the part of any six men who can make out a prima facie case, to obtain a commission of inquiry, has a tendency to make men careful in their actions; and one of the most forceful illustrations of the effect of the legislation passed last session is the very circumstance that since that legislation has been put on the statute-book we have not had the outcries against mergers and combinations that we heard before, and that it has not been found necessary up to the present time, except in one or two cases, to endeavour to start proceedings under this statute.
But, Sir, even if my hon. friend had made out a case as to why the government should appoint a royal commission for the purpose suggested, I would contend that he has chosen an inopportune time for his proposal. At this moment this country is engaged in a consideration of one of the largest commercial transactions which it has ever had to consider. Any proposed change in tariff arrangements is always viewed with a good deal of anxiety by all classes in the community. At the present
moment the United States and Canada are each considering what legislation they shall pass in respect to a number of commodities, some of which are being produced by these very mergers to which my hon. friend refers. Now, I ask him, as a man of wide public experience, whether he thinks that at such a time it would be a wise thing for the government of this country to announce to the public that it proposed to appoint a royal commission for the purpose of making an inquiry into various business interests in this country.
I am afraid that the effect of adopting the course which my hon. friend suggests would be to bring about a condition of affairs diametrically opposite to that which he himself desires. What could more affect the securities of some of the large business concerns in Canada than an announcement to the public to-morrow, or the day after, that the government of this country, for reasons which had been disclosed in this parliament, had found it necessary to appoint a royal commission to investigate some of these large industrial establishments? Would it not have a baneful effect upon the securities of this country abroad? I think that when my hon. friend considers the matter carefully, he will come to the conclusion that it would; and if he looks more carefully at the effect of the. legislation which is at present on. the statute-book. I think he will see that that legislation is one of the strongest safeguards this nation has for the reputation of its securities. The fact that it is known throughout the world that if our large industrial concerns seek to do -what is not proper, seek to take an unfair advantage of the consumers, seek to unduly enhance prices or restrict competition, any six persons may start the machinery of government at work and secure a full and complete investigation into the business of such concerns the knowledge of the existence of such legislation has an influence abroad which tends to give the securities of these companies a value they otherwise would not have. In the reasons my hon. friend has urged, he has failed to make out a satisfactory case why in the public interests the course he has suggested should be taken; and I am convinced that on further reflection he will agree that it would be very much against the public interest to adopt that course.
In conclusion let me say that I hope none of the remarks I have ventured to make will be construed as in any way minimizing the importance of publicity in the work of these large organizations. I feel that in the public interest too great facilities for reasonable investigation at any moment cannot be afforded, I agree entirely with my hon. friend as to the importance of public investigation of mergers, and it was in that view that we put on our

statutes last year the Combines Investigation Act; but where I disagree with him is with regard to the case he has made out as affording reasons why a public investigation should take place, .and as to the opportuneness of such an investigation at this particular time. My hon. friend referred to the number of combines or mergers which have taken place recently. Well, this is an age of combinations. Not only do we see large combinations in matter? commercial, but also in cither directions. Even the churches have begun to combine.

Does the hon. gentleman think it is very proper for him to designate the movement for church union as a combine?
. Mr. KING. It was with no invidious intention that I used the word ' combine,' and certainly I did not use it in the sense the hon. gentleman indicates. I certainly would regard the proposed union of the churches as a consolidation, and I was pointing out that this was an .age of great consolidations in all lines, and in that connection I alluded to the church union movement as one that might possibly be more remote from the minds of hon. gentlemen opposite than the others I have named. We have large organizations of capital and large organizations of labour.
Speaking with regard to the merging of capital, we have to recognize that this being an age of competition, consolidation is in some respects very desirable. As my hon. friend has said, mergers in themselves are not necessarily a bad thing, and I think he will agree with me when I say that large consolidations in this age of competition are sometimes necessary, because the competition is not merely between one industry and another, but frequently between the industries of one nation and those of another, even the industries of one continent and those of another. The fact is that economic conditions have so developed that these large consolidations are becoming essential to the industrial expansion of a nation, and just because large consolidations are becoming more numerous inevitable for this very reason there should be a means of investigation at hand all the time, as afforded by the legislation enacted and not investigations for a special occasion only, as is suggested by my hon. friend.
Is it the hon. gentleman's opinion that these mergers and combines tend to reduce prices or increase them to the consumer.
Have there been any investigations under this Act to which my hon. friend refers or applications for investigations?

I might, say that at present there is an application pending before Mr. Justice Cannon in Quebec for the appointment of a board to inquire into an alleged combine in the case of the United Shoe Machinery Company. That application, I believe, is under consideration, and we are likely to hear any day

whether it has been granted or not. There have been a large number of inquiries as to proceedings under the Act. But I am a little afraid that many persons have not as yet come to know the full significance of that measure, or to understand its completeness. It tnay be that some of the representations made by gentlemen opposite while the measure was under discussion in the House, as to its possible limitations has had an influence on the minds of some. But I think it is quite true that, once the measure is tested, it will be found effective. And, as I have already said, the absence of cases under this Act does not by any means prove that it has not been of efficient service in restraining large organizations from taking a course that otherwise they might have been tempted to take.
Was a registrar appointed under the Act, and if so, who is he?
Yes, Mr. Acland, the Deputy Minister of Labour, was appointed registrar.

Had I not known that it was the Minister of Labour who was speaking I would have thought it was the minister of combines. Practically, his speech is a defence of these mergers. I would also make the criticism that he has evaded the question presented here to-night, the question of regulating the capitalization of public companies, which is one of the pressing questions of the day. I had intended to take up that question this afternoon in connection with the railways, and I will take it up at the first opportunity. The disorganized condition of affairs in the United States to-day is largely due to faults in connection with the securities issued in that country. But a commission, exactly equal to a royal commission, has been appointed by President Taft to ascertain how the capitalization of railways is to be regulated. That commission is made up of most eminent men, headed by Prof. Hadley. If our securities to-day are good in the markets of the old country, and they are, and if the securities of the United States are not marketable in Europe, as is the case, what is the reason? It is that Americans have overworked the market; they have issued so much watered stock, they have capitalized their great trusts and railways to such an extent, that they can no longer market the securities. And if we pursue a similar method our securities will be in disrepute in Europe in a short time. You cannot have the flotation of securities referred to by the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk), you cannot have ' high finance ' without damaging the credit of the country. See what the late Mr. Harriman did in connection with the
railways in which he was interested. He suddenly became the greatest railway man in the country. And he attained that position by manipulating the securities of the railways. One of the great grievances of the state of California is that a wholly unnecessary $10,000,000 a year has been added to the freight rates of that country in order to pay dividends on watered securities issued by Mr. Harriman. When a Minister of Labour says that the AntiCombines Bill meets the case he himself does not meet the case, for the Anti-Combines Bill has nothing to do with regulating the issue of securities. When I come to discuss that, in connection with the Tail-ways I think I shall be able to make out my case.
Referring to the banking system, which was mentioned by the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk), I will deal with that more fully when we take up the banking law. But it is evident that some of our banks have become what may be called flotation banks-they devote their resources more, to the flotation of companies than to giving accommodation to the public. One of the dangers of our banking system is in the flotation of these securities. But that subject^ will come up in connection with the banking law. It is a fact, as the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) said in introducing his motion, that the rate of interest has gone up because of these neiv methods of finance. You cannot get anybody now to entertain an ordinary mortgage as security. The investor is looking for bonds or preferred stock accompanied by these free gifts of common stock as a bonus. And all this new trade of promoter and promotions is based on the idea of the overissue of securities to be loaded on the public, the interest on which is transferred to the consumer, whether a customer of the railway or a user of the goods produced by combines. And it is a fact that combines to-day are responsible for the increased cost of living now complained of in the United States. I think nobody will deny that. And reciprocity, or anything else, will not reduce prices unless you control and regulate the capitalization of mergers. This will have to be done by some public law, and such a law can be drafted only after investigation. The Minister of Labour told us that our trade was increasing and the banks had more deposits than ever. But that increase is no greater than our increase of population. The need of the country is more capital. When the Minister of Labour says that the law to regulate combines is a cure for the great public grievance of over-capitalization of companies that exists he evades the issue that must be faced. Canada, if she would avoid the evils of high finance and

the condition of affairs in the United States, must regulate the issue of securities by all public companies. Promoters will-as I have known in some cases-take a concern of $500,000 and capitalize it at $3,000,000, and put the stock on the market, making a large profit out of it, though, eventually, those who buy the securities may not get their interest. In the meantime, the public is loaded with the stock, and there is a tendency toward combination in order to increase prices. We boast of our Companies' Act, but nearly all the iniquities in connection with financial affairs, whether in America or Europe, grow out of the Companies' Act and the right it confers to issue shares. And, unless there is the strictest regulation by law of the issue of securities, the same kind of injury to the .public and to the credit of the country is bound to follow. Therefore, I would like to see in this country the same kind of commission appointed as in the United States to investigate and bring out the facts. I am awaiting with great interest that report, which will be made some time next summer by Prof. Hadley and his associates in connection with the capitalization of railways in the United States. In a little while it is probable that the United States will take up the question in a wider aspect, and will devise some wav to bring out the facts and secure regulation. When Governor Woodrow Wilson made his inaugural speech the other day in New Jersey he said one of the principal objects of his administration would be the regulation of the issue of securities, and that he intended, if possible, to put a stop to the discredit that had come upon that state by the result of the issue of powers of incorporation of all kinds, which he declared was a crying evil, not only in the state, but in the whole nation. So the question is before us, it must be dealt with, and it cannot be handled by a law that is merejy directed against combinations.

It has long seemed to me that one of the greatest problems with which this parliament has to deal is this very question. Whether we will ever reach the day when parliament will be able to devise laws to control these combinations-, I am not prepared to say. At any rate, there is great need for some other legislation on the subject, it cannot come an hour too soon, and in my judgment we have already delayed too long in finding a solution. We see the evil in the financial world, we see it amongst manufacturing corporations, we find it in these large trusts. Other countries appear to be troubled with it as well as Canada and the United States, and they have endeavoured, but very ineffectively so far, to provide a Mr. MACLEAN.
remedy for the evil. At one time I had great hopes that President Roosevelt would break up many of these combinations. He started an action against the Sugar Trust, and he certainly woke them up pretty well. The publicity which he gave to their nefarious transactions, partially at least restrained that trust in its operations. The Oil Trust was another combination of a similar kind. He attempted to attack them, but unfortunately, owing to his presidential term expiring, he was unable to do the good work which he would undoubtedly have done if he had remained longer in office. I felt sure from his conduct that he would not be reelected, because I believed that the trusts and combines, and mergers, and railway corporations he was attacking would be too powerful in their opposition to allow him to be re-elected. I regret to notice that his successor, President Taft, is not following in the lines of President Roosevelt, although he declared that he intended to pursue his policy. I am afraid he has already been restrained, and I do not expect henceforth to hear of him accomplishing much.
Now, the hon. the Minister of Labour praises his combines law. At first glance it seems to be very well designed. But I think our experience since it was enacted proves the correctness of the predictions that were made at the time the Bill was discussed, namely, that there would be very few applications for investigation under it. Why? Because, as the old saying is, what is everybody 'rf business is nobody's business. If you leave it to six independent citizens of this country to put the law in motion, knowing as they must know, the trouble they will bring upon themselves by becoming practically the prosecutors, knowing as they must the risk, the danger and the abuse they will bring upon themselves in attempting to prosecute a combination, there is probably not one case in a hundred where the men can be found to undertake the task.. I believe that has been the trouble. The minister said no investigations have taken place. There is one pending somewhere down in Quebec, he said, but he did not tell us where it was, or what it was about.

I beg the hon. gentleman's pardon. I said it was against the United Shoe Machinery Company, and the application had been made in the city of Quebec. The application was presented at the close of last year, there was an appeal, and judgment was reserved on the 1st of February, and may be given out any day now.

I did not hear the name of the case. But the Minister of Labour

said that this government had been striv-i ing to stop the nefarious operations of these combines. He said other methods that had been adopted up to the present time were not successful, therefore they were obliged to devise some other means to battle with these evils, and that was the combines law. He mentioned first that the Criminal Code was amended so that they might be attacked, but that was not effective. I would like to ask him why it is not effective? Because, after the Bill was put through in this House it was amended in the Senate until it was of no use. It was introduced a second time in this House and amended so as to make it valuable, but it dropped out because there was not time to put it through that session. It was introduced again and passed as amended so that would make it useful and so that it could be enforced.
' What year was that?

I think it was about 1900. The law then could be put in force, and under it convictions could he secured against parties who were violating it. But what does the government do? They amended it the next session, by reenacting the words struck out which left it as it originally was, and thereby made it worthless. That was the opinion of the late Sir Oliver Mowat, and he was regarded as a very able lawyer; he gave that as a reason why the law was of no avail. For what purpose ? I honestly believe and 1 always did believe that it was at the instigation of these people who are carrying on their improper dealings that the then Minister of Justice when amending the Criminal Code put it back again. Now the Minister of Labour says that it was of no use. They made it of no use. They made it so that practically it is impossible for it to be of any value.

Did the Minister of Justice of that day-I think it was Sir John Thompson-express the opinion in regard to the legislation to which the hon. gentleman (Mr. Sproule.) now refers that (parliament was not enacting anything new or anything which was not already law, that they were not providing any penalty that did not already exist in the common law ; in other words, that the whole legislation that they proposed really amounted to nothing? Was not that opinion then expressed?
Not at all. He said that he did not think it went much further than the general law went at that time.
What was the object of introducing this legislation at all?

It was to focus public attention on these particular Acts and to
provide a remedy and a punishment. It was because an attack was made upon this law that Sir John Thompson gave the opinion that under the law of the time you might institute a prosecution, and probably carry it on as effectually to the end as you could under this amendment but owing to "the fact that nobody ever pretended to put the criminal law in motion for that purpose. This law was specifically providing a penalty for certain offences which were enumerated. I would further say that what always attracted my attention was the fact that the law was amended so as to make it of no value because the government immediately amended it, put it back again, left it absolutely useless and it has remained so from that day to this.
The Minister of Labour said : We have another provision ; we have a provision in the 'Customs Act, and the present government put it there in order to show their desire to control these nefarious combinations and trusts. That was to the effect that with regard to any article that was the subject of a combine or a trust to the detriment of the consumer or producer, and it might appear so to the government, they could take the customs duty off that article, let it come in free and thus punish the parties in that way. I have several times in this House heard members of the government eulogize that law and say what a wonderful thing they had done in that they had made it so simple, so easy for the government to set the law in motion in order to punish parties who committed this offence, and in order that the consumer might get his goods at the least possible price. Although their attention was drawn over and over again to certain'articles that were the subject of such combines, and an appeal was made to them to take these cases up, thev absolutely refused, year after year, to ' move. Judge Garrow prepared a case and presented it to the government before he was put on the bench, and afterwards placed it in the hands of others who presented it in this House, and although their attention was drawn to it not once or twice but many times and many respectable firms in this country were being injuriously affected and the government were asked to apply this provision of the customs law and punish the parties they absolutely refused to put the Act in motion and it remained a dead letter. They did it in one instance with regard to paper and that is the only time they ever put it into motion. Had it not been for the fact that this happened to he something that was pinching the press, and they were; afraid of the .power of the press I believe they never would have touched it. So, that law has remained a dead letter up to the present time except in that one instance. Then, the Minister of Labour introduces bis

Combines Act, and lie eulogize-s that to a certain, extent. The minister referred to a speech that I made away back in 1898 with regard to the danger of putting it in the power of the government to send out a commission in these cases. I always thought there was a great deal of merit in it but that there was a good deal of danger also, and when I came to see what the present government did in other lines 1 frankly confess that I felt it would not be a safe thing to do in the interest of the people because-I would be very much afraid that they might throw out threats, if they wanted to control certain great corporations in their own interests, or that there would be some intimations given that they might look out or. there would be danger ahead for them. If it should turn out that they would take the law up and enforce it honestly and properly, I think it would be valuable, but from what we have seen with regard to their conduct in other lines in my , judgment the public of this country would have no confidence in their desire to put that law into force honestly and properly.
Does not the hon. gentleman approve of the suggestion of the Son. member for Jacques Cartier that a commission should be appointed?
I am not talking about the proposal of the hon. member for Jacq-ues Cartier >at all. I am talking about the quotation which the hon. Minister of Labour made from what I said in 1898.
The proposition we are considering is as to whether the same course suggested then should be adopted now.

I am giving my reasons why the people distrust the government. I have given the various powers that they have had in their hands, and which they have never used, and I have said that I would be afraid that they would use the one I referred to either not at all or for blackmailing purposes or probably for the purpose of raising subscriptions to run elections.
Does the hon. gentleman approve of the appointing of a royal commission for this purpose?
I have not said whether I do or do not.
Will you please say?

The minister may or he may not be a lawyer. Lawyers always want one to say ' yes/ or ' no/ I could put a great many 'questions to the hon. gentleman. For instance, I might ask him if it is true that he has stopped beating his wife.
Unfortunately, I have no wife.

I was attempting, in answer to the comment of the hon. gentleman, to give the reasons for the position I took on this question, I am not dealing with the motion before the House so much as referring to the quotation which the minister made from a former speech of mine, and I am saying that the government have not honestly, in my judgment, taken any action for the purpose of punishing these individuals or stopping those combines.
