That is the reason I am referring to the quotation which the minister made from my remarks in 1898.

Apart altogether from the past, would the hon. gentleman allow me to ask him one question? Does he approve at the present moment of the government appointing a royal commission for the purpose of inquiring into mergers as moved for by the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk)?

I have not read the motion close enough. I read it very cursorily, but it does not) commend itself strongly to my mind because I do not think that it goes far enough in its scope. But, I would like to see some independent commission to take up these subjects with authority to deal with them, and not leave it to a private citizen to do it at great trouble and expense to himself for which he is not indemnified. If I were to talk about my views on a royal commission it would require a much more lengthy explanation than I desire to enter upon with reference to this motion to-night. I have always thought that the government were not serious with regard to this matter. I think still that they are not serious about it. It is like their eight-hour labour day, it is a gold brick handed out to the people to deceive them. I said so about that Bill when it was enacted, I think so about it yet, and until the government show some desire to put the law in motion I shall continue to think so.

It is apparent to every one who has considered the subject that there may be combinations for business purposes which are entirely legitimate and which are not attended with any improper or injurious consequences to the community as a whole. Of that we can see examples around us every clay in Canada. On the other hand there is not only in Canada, but in other countries, a tendency to combinations of a character which are not for the advantage of the community or of the country. These combinations may be roughly divided into two classes:	those which are created for
the purpose of excluding competition and raising prices, and those the capitalization of which is very exaggerated. We know of cases where a great deal of the

capitalization does not represent any actual investment or anything in the nature of tangible value, but merely what might be called potential future profits. When a country is carrying on its affairs under a protective system, it is easy to 'see there may be evil in that because when stock representing no actual investment reaches the hands of bona fide holders for value, there may be a demand more or less insistent that the people who paid money for this stock- which originally represented no money at all-should have some claim on those in charge of the fiscal system of the country, so that dividends may be earned upon this stock. On a recent occasion outside of this House, I stated that I believed a good deal of injury had been done to the industrial development of Canada by some transactions of that character, and, gentlemen who are interested in manufactures afterwards said to me that they realized that there was a good deal of truth in my statement, because, as I said then and as I repeat now, when retribution comes for practices of that kind the punishment is apt to fall upon the just and the unjust alike. Combinations, even of the character to which I first referred, do not always have the absolute result of raising prices. One of the world's greatest combinations, the Standard Oil Company, did I understand reduce prices. I am not justifying the existence of that great combine; I am merely citing it as an illustration of the possibility of having perhaps an improper combine and at the same time a reduction instead of an increase in price. It is abundantly evident, not only in Canada but the United States, that combinations created for the purpose of doing away with competition do increase the price of commodities beyond what it should be. These two evils; the attempt to shut out competition and the capitalization of future possible profits are evils to which the attention of parliament may very well be directed. The Minister of Labour is perfectly satisfied with the existing legislation, but I am not sure that it meets the case at all. To be perfectly frank I do not think it does. In the_ first place, even if it were effective there is no provision which imposes upon any particular authority the duty of enforcing it. In the words of the homely adage quoted by my hon. friend (Mr. Sproule) what is everybodv's business is nobody's business and, a private person in this country will not take upon himself the odium and responsibility, not to speak of the expense, of enforcing such a law. It is idle for the government to place such a measure upon the statute-book and not to provide for its enforcement. I would dismiss altogether from consideration the operation of that statute, because I am of the present opinion that it would never result in coping with the two evils I have pointed out.	,
There is another thing that should not be lost sight of-we have absolute power in this parliament, if we exercise it, to enact legislation which will make the continued existence of these two evils impossible, so far of course, as that can be attained in view of the infinite resourcefulness of the men who are creating them, and in view also of the enormous complexity of business transactions in these later days. We may not be able to provide an absolutely perfect remedy but this parliament can at least provide a reasonable remedy. We are face to face also with the existence of these great combines in the United States upon a scale much larger than has been attempted in Canada. The combination of business interests in the United States at the present day, was undreamed of 15 vears ago, or even 10 years ago, and their influence is making itself felt in Canada. There are in Canada at the present time several branches of industry the output of which, and the prices at which the output shall be sold in Canada, are absolutely regulated by direct and positive orders from great corporations in the United States. I am not speaking from personal knowledge now, but from what has been conveyed to me by men who ought to be in a thoroughly good position to know what they are speaking of, and as to whose absolute truthfulness I have not the slightest shadow of a doubt.
My hon. friend from West Lambton (Mr. Pardee), says the same thing is true of combinations in Canada. I was not aware of that, because my attention has been directed to the remarkable circumstance that there were combines in the United States regulating, by direct and positive orders, the amount of output of Canadian factories, and the price at which that output should be sold. If that is the case, it seems to me that that subject, although it may ibe a very difficult one to deal with, and one that possibly can only be dealt with by means of the tariff, is a subject that requires the consideration of this parliament, and that ought to be taken up in connection with the evils resulting from combinations having their origin in this country, I think my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier has done no more than his duty in bringing this subject to the attention of the House. Whether or not we agree with the remedy he proposes, whether or not we agree with the terms in which he has couched his resolution, I think we all must admit that he has done a public service in bringing the subject to the attention of parliament. For my part, I am inclined to think that instead of investigation wre want, some legislation. I am inclined to think that parliament is at _the present *time possessed of about all the information necessary to enable us to put some legislation on the Statute Book of Canada.

i Mr. F. F. PARDEE (West Lambton), Mr. Speaker, from listening to the -various opinions that have been expressed regarding the Combines Investigation Act, _ it becomes apparent what a difficult subject this is to deal with. Nobody will deny that under existing conditions in many lines the combines are an absolute menace to the people, having the effect of enhancing prices. The prime object, therefore, of any measure that may be brought into force should be to remedy that evil. The hon. leader of the Opposition has said that there is now sufficient machinery, irrespective of the Act at present under discussion, to get at the basis of the evil. If that is the case, I am bound to say that I am quite ignorant of it. I have given considerable attention to this matter, having taken some interest in the passing of that Act, and up to the time that Act was passed, I did not see any remedy for the evil complained of. It is true, the Act is not perfect, but what I would like to know, is how it can be made more perfect. It Eas been said that there is no way of enforcing the penalties that may be incurred under this Act. The ordinary way I understand, is simply by suit. In what other way can it be done ?
I might call the attention of my hon. friend to the fact that the Act makes provision that the Governor in Council may enforce the penalties.

I did not know that that was provided in the Act. The hon. leader of the Opposition speaks of the expense required to put the Act in motion; but one [DOT] of the strongest points in favour of the Act is that the expense is borne entirely by the government.
I think the initial expense must be borne by the complainant until the case goes from the hands of the judge into the hands of the Commission.

That is merely the making of the motion. If the motion is successful, the costs are borne entirely by the government. The fault found by the farmers with the old procedure was this: It is very well to say. that there is at present a provision in the statute whereby we may attack combines, and if certain things are shown certain remedies will be given, but how is it possible for us to get together and put up the whole cost of wljat. may be a very expensive investigation, as was shown by the paper combine investigation. That is almost an impossibility for us. Therefore, it was that section 41 of the Combines Investigation Act was adopted, which provided that all the expense connected with the investigation should be paid by the government, and not a single dollar is to come out of the complainant.
I beg the hon. gentleman's pardon. If the judge orders proof or inquiry on the first motion, the expense of it has to be borne by the complainant, and it may be quite costly.
Only for the pTima facie case.
If this is a public evil, why should any responsibility of that kind be imposed upon private individuals ? If this is a good law why should not public provision be made for its enforcement ?

That question was brought up at the time this Act was under investigation. It appears to me to be selfevident why. I think it would not be wise for this House to put into the hands of any one, perhaps an irresponsible person, and without the slightest ground of- complaint, the means of coming day after day and setting all the machinery of this Act in motion on an ex parte motion.

But all that is not necessary. If there is a great evil of this kind, surely vou can appoint an officer or form a tribunal, who will not be called upon to act upon the initiative of any person, but who will be bound and responsible to take the initiative and deal with this evil wherever reasonable evidence exists that an inquiry ought to be made.

Practically we are agreed upon that. That is practically the same thing as now exists. Their complaint and evidence before any commission that might be appointed. Surely the commission could not investigate holus bolus without having so'me evidence on which to base its action.

The Railway Commission of Canada can, upon its own initiative, make any investigation it sees fit, wherever in its opinion, an evil exists, and I see no reason whatever why the same principle might not be applied to such a case as .this.

I can hardly agree with my hon. friend as to that. It would be giving a commission too great power to allow it, on its own initiative, to walk into the office of any business concern and examine its books and go into all the details of its transactions. To grant such a power to any body of men, which they might put into effect whatever they chose without even any demand being made upon them, could not fail to work injustice in some cases. As concerns the argument of the hon. member for Grey (Mr. Sproule), what he desires is an independent commission and not have the onus put upon private individuals, because these individuals who would lay a complaint might be made to suffer in many ways. But sure-

ly no commission could be more independent than the one intended to be created by the Act now on our statutes. Those who complain appoint a representative, those who are complained against appoint a second, and a third is appointed by the courts. Surely no commission .could be more independent than that. Each side is entitled to employ its own counsel. I fail to see why any six farmers should have any reason to bear persecution in any way because they happen to lay a complaint, and I do not think there could be any doubt about their readiness to prosecute their complaint if they thought they could make out a prima facie case. Therefore I do not see how we could create any commission more independent than the one contemplated by the Act.
If the hon. gentleman were one of the six farmers he would think differently.

I do not see why I should. I have talked to a good many of the farmers on this matter and my information from them differs from that of my hon. friend. But so far as my hon. friend's remarks go, he is distinctly not in favour of the resolution of the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) because he said very frankly-and I admire him for his frankness-that he does not think this government could appoint any commission which would not in some way do something wrong, and consequently could not be de. pended upon to act justly.

I did not say that as far as my recollection goes, and I certainly did not intend to say it. What I intended to say was that if any commission were directly under the control of the government, the government could make that commission act or refrain from acting, and I would have very grave suspicion that the evil would not be effectively dealt with.

Well, I take it that the motion of the hon. member for Jacques Cartier, if it means anything, means that the commission should be appointed by the government. I cannot see any other way in which the commission he recommends could be appointed. I am not here in any way to defend combines. To my mind they are a menace. My hon. friend from Jacques Cartier has pointed out in his resolution that very frequently they raise the prices. That no one can doubt. But the sole point to my mmd is this What is the best way to get at the evil and stamp it out? This resolution, to my mind, is certainly not sufficient, and I have failed to hear any one propose anything that would provide a more effective remedy than the one we have on our statutes. But should a better remedy be found than is on our statutes, I am pre-94
pared to support it. As I have said however, the opinions expressed to-night as to the regulation of capitalization and various other things only go to show that so far nothing more effective has been proposed than we already have. My hon. friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden) has himself said that the legislation he evidently had in his mind might not be perfect because of the many devious ways of these combines which might render it unworkable. That is only another argument to show that in any new legislation such as now proposed, the House will not get at the root of the evil, and the only thing to do is to put in operation the legislation we have. What is there to prevent, under the existing statute, an application being made and a commission or board of arbitration being appointed? Under that statute the various parties to the dispute can have their own counsel and thresh the matter out. The Act goes so far as to say that the books of the corporation may be examined into by the board of arbitration, and this board of arbitration may be started practically without a single _ dollar of expense to the parties complaining. The chief objection I have to the motion of the hon. member for Jacques Cartier is this, that having spent the time we did on the Combines Investigation Act last session and that, in so far as we can judge at present, that legislation is better than any yet proposed, I can see no reason why we should devise some new tribunal and appoint another commission to examine into the very thing covered by the present Act. If any legislation can be shown which will more effectively reach the object which it is intended to reach I shall be only too glad to support it, but I do not think that any has been proposed so far. As the hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) has said these combines can be waked up just as well by our present Act as by any other legislation and therefore the resolution of the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) is simply a surplusage; and before deciding any other remedy, we ought to give fair opportunity to test the one we have.

The speech of my hon. friend from West Lambton (Mr. Pardee) is a confirmation of the general opinion that the government is unable to reach these combines. I am sure nobody in Canada will think for a moment that we have not sufficient legislation on our statutes.
The hon. leader of the opposition did.

The complaint about the country is that the Minister ot Labour is devoting altogether too much time in the preparation of legislation and fails to enforce the legislation already on the statutes.



The reason there is so much talk in the country about combines is because of the introduction of the national policy many years ago and tjie attacks my hon. friends opposite made on that policy. My hon. friends opposite taught the people of Canada that combines were introduced by the policy of the Liberal-Conservative government. My hon. friend the Minister of Customs (Mr. Paterson) was one of those who went about telling the people what a wicked policy the Conservative party had created, and that it was the prolific parent of combines, and that these combines had unduly enhanced prices to the consumer, and when the Liberals . came into power of course these combines would be immediately got rid of. The people are to-day asking how is it that this government does not enforce the legislation it has and break up the combines which are unduly enhancing prices. It looks as if my hon. friends opposite, by their tariff reform and by sitting in their offices preparing legislation, were trying to reach this great question when they are well aware that all that is wanted is some activity on the part of some officer who should be appointed for that purpose, as my hon. friend the leader of the opposition suggested when this matter was up for discussion last year. The Minister of Labour had a year of trial of his new legislation, and he acknowledges to-night that it has done nothing except create one case.

If I may interrupt my hon. friend, I did not acknowledge that the legislation has done nothing; on the contrary, I say it has done everything. The very fact that there are no investigations under it shows that these companies are held under restraint by it.

The hon. gentleman seems to say that because the legislation has done nothing, therefore, it has done everything. Because there is only one case under the law, the hon. gentleman tells us that peace is abroad, and there are no combines.
I would remind my hon. friend of the illustration I used: He would not estimate the effect of the death penalty by the number of hangings, but by the fewness of them.

I would like to hear the hon. gentleman explain how this law has kept down combines. Only in one case has any action been taken under it. And the hon. gentleman admits that he and his department, and the government have taken no action at all. If inactivity will reach difficulties of this kind, it is the only case in which difficulties are to be dealt with in that way. The people will not be satisfied, and are not satisfied. The defence of existing legislation 'by my hon. friend is Mr. BLAIN.
practically a plea for combines. Take, for instance, the situation in relation to ibeef. This session, and more particularly last session, complaint was made from this side of the House that in western Canada there is a great evil that is hindering the agricultural interests there, and that in sections of Manitoba, and the other provinces where, years ago, a large number of cattle were raised by the farmers, these people have gone out of the cattle business for the reason that there are low prices for their beef because of the operations of a combine. And it is proven that in the province of Ontario the price paid for beef to the farmers is not an excessive price; no one can accuse the agricultural interest of charging too much for the beef produced upon our farms. The difficulty arises after the beef has been sold by the farmer and before it reaches the consumer. There are combines in that business; the Minister of Labour himself understands that. There has been discussion in the public press, and, no doubt, the Department of Labour has received considerable complaint from the people of the country that this legislation does not cure the evil. There has been legislation on the statute-book for a long time. There is a law that was placed on the statute-book at the instance of the late Hon. Clarke Wallace. I am not saying that it was well enforced; it is not necessary that I should discuss or defend it. _ But when the present government came into power they promised that better legislation would be passed and enforced. But the Minister of Customs (Mr. Paterson) of course, sits quietly by and you do not get a word against combines from him. All that he does is to reform tariffs
Hear, hear.
And he could not reform tariffs if he had not supporters like hon. gentlemen opposite at his back. He does not have to consult them ; they will vote.
Hear, hear.
Perfectly satisfied.

I have listened for some years to my hon. friend from Carleton (Mr. Carvell) talk about the importance of stability of tariffs in this country. Yet when all interests are doing very well, the government take up the question of tariffs^
That was in the National Policy too.

The Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugsley) will endorse it, because it contains a sort of balm of Gilead for every part of the country. However, we are not discussing the tariff question just now. I point out that there is a strong feeling in this country against combines, that enhance prices of staple com-

modities to the consumer. The leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden, Halifax), has pointed out that there are great combines already in existence in Canada, combines that are provincial and combines that are national also. And there are combines from the old country, huge combines such as this country never heard of. There would be no need of the resolution of my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) if this government had been doing their duty to the people on this line. My hon. friend (Mr. Monk) would support the government, and this side of the House has supported the government, in legislation proposed for the purpose of preventing the formation of these combines. The Minister of Labour in his Bill of last session had the united support of both sides of the House. I pointed out at the time that I did not think this legislation would reach the case. I do not think the Minister of Labour himself thought it would reach the case.
Certainly, I did. Why did the hon. gentleman (Mr. Blain) support it if he thought it would not reach the case?
I pointed out that it would not reach the case.
Why did my hon. friend support it if he thought it would not rqaeh the case?

I take the ground that the government in power are responsible to the people for the legislation of this parliament. Whenever there is anything good, my hon. friend says: See what we have been doing for Canada! But whenever there is anything going wrong he says: Oh the opposition are as much responsible as we are, Sir, I do not think the people will be satisfied with that kind of argument, I want to point out that this question is one that should receive the energetic attention of the government; it is their duty to look into it seriously. It is not enough for the Minister of Labour to say, as the hon. member for West Lambton did, that five or six farmers could join together and make a complaint, and that if the machinery of this law was put in force under this complaint these combines could be reached and the government would pay all the costs. That is not sufficient. If the government believe that this law is able to reach these combines, it is their duty to appoint somebody whose business it will be to enforce the law, otherwise the legislation is a dead letter. Why does not the hon. gentleman accept the suggestion of the leader of the opposition, and appoint an officer in his department to enforce the law?
94i

The reason why I think such a course would hardly commend itself to the House is that when a similar line of action was recommended once before it was pointed out that the government would use such an officer for its own purposes; they would send him as an agent to further political ends. To follow the argument used by the hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule), this officer would oppose those interests which the government might think it desirable to oppose, and refrain from opposing favourable interests. The legislation which has been put upon the statute-book removes the possibility .of anything of that kind, and leaves the initiative in the operation of the law to those who are likely to be affected adversely.

If my hon. friend's suggestion has anything in it, it is that there cannot be found in his department any one to enforce this legislation because there is too much politics in it. That is a strange condition of things. That rather suggests that my hon. friend knows that he is possibly surrounding himself in his department with politicians rather than with men who will enforce the labour law. I am not saying that is the case, because I accept his statement. He says it would not do to accept the suggestion of the leader of the opposition, for the reason that if such an officer was appointed he would be charged with enforcing legislation against ope class of people, and leaving another class go free. Does the hon. gentleman think that is a sufficient answer to the suggestion made by the leader of the opposition?
Would you not be rather apt to make that charge yourself.

Mv hon. friend has been guilty so long, in his early days, of looking after the interest of his party rather than the interest of his country, that I fear his vision is not very clear on a question of this kind. I want to point out that there is a feeling abroad in Canada that combines are in active existence. That feeling disturbs commercial conditions, and agricultural interests as well. If the people could be convinced that where combines are proved to exist this government would scatter them; that where it was proved that prices were enhanced unduly in consequence of these combines the government would suppress them; then the people would be satisfied and content, instead of being suspicious and discontented as at present. When people are paying too much for their goods at any time they want a government in power who will break down the combines, and who will see to it that the manufacturers shall not be permitted to charge more than a fair and reasonable

price for their goods. But so long as the government allow these combines to continue their operations, with the effect of unduly enhancing prices to the consumer, there will always continue to be these discussions, and these unsettled relations between the manufacturer and the consumer. That is a point that ought to receive some attention at the hands of the Minister of Labour, and that is what I had understood his department was for. When I open the ' Gazette,' published by the Department of Labour, and look over the difficulties that occur between capital and labour I find that they are mainly settled by themselves, not by the agency of _ the minister's department. My hon. friend seems to think that when he has put a law upon the statute-book his work is done, and that somebody else must enforce it. A law of that kind will not be satisfactory. I am in accord with my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) when he directs attention to the condition of things that exists in this country at the present time. I say that if the Minister of Labour hopes to reach these difficulties that exist in Canada he must be more active, not in putting legislation upon the statute-book, but in enforcing the legislation that is already upon the statute-book.

I confess I had expected that a question of this importance would have received more attention from the government. I am very much disappointed with my hon. and young friend the Minister of Labour (Mr. King), because he does not seem to have accomplished the results in his department that we hq.d a right to expect. No doubt the hon. gentleman is very busy in his department, and I can understand that possibly questions of this kind do not absorb so much of his atten: tion as they do outside the House. But, really, some of the motives given by him for not accepting the prayer of this motion seem to be trivial. He suggests that it would be most untimelv for us to investigate mergers at this moment, because negotiations are going on with the United States for a reciprocity treaty. Surely my hon. friend is not serious. What possible relation is there between a proposal to investigate our economic conditions in Canada and the negotiations for a modification of our tariff with the United States?
In order to give some color to my hon. friends suggestion, he says that we would have to investigate the businesses of these companies. My hon. friend is not serious as to that. This motion calls for the investigation of the circumstances attending the merger, the influence that it has in connection with prices and the influence in our standing in foreign markets and banking necessities. We have nothing to do with Mr. BLAIN.
the details of the businesses of these companies. Not at all, but a Royal Commission, formed under the terms of this motion, if it were passed, would not be called upon to look into the details of any business whatever, or I much misunderstand the purport of the motion. My hon. friend seems to think that the object of this motion is to complain of the price of certain commodities, such as is contemplated by the Combines Act, to complain of the increase in the price of say, butter, or any other such necessities of life. There is nothing of that kind in the motion, and I think it would be sufficient for me to mention that any lawyer would see that the combine Act does not apply to an object of this kind. In order to be able to assume that that is proven it is sufficient to read section 5 of the Act passed last year under, the leadership of my hon. friend, because you will see that it merely applies to certain specific cases of arrangements between producers as to the prices of their products, There is nothing of that in this motion. While I am speaking of that, I may say that I was amused to hear the minister say that the passing of this Act had stopped combines.
No, I beg your pardon.
Yes, the hon. gentleman compared it with the death penalty.

No, my hon. friend is mistaken. I spoke of its adverse effect on combinations. I did not say that they had at all ceased because I believe that combines will continue to increase during the coming years. But, I did say that it had had a restraining effect upon combines using ;their power in a manner detrimental to the public.

Surely my hon. friend knows that these combines have been continuing during the whole year, that regularly, manufacturers and wholesale and retail dealers have been meeting as usual, fixing prices and violating the terms of the Act. There is no doubt that the Act applies a remedy, but as the hon. member for Grey (Mr. Sproule), said, it is a useless remedy, because nobody will employ it. In truth, no government, as my hon.. friend from Grey says, will take up this question seriously and directly. Why ? Because it affects great interests and governments are afraid to touch these interests. There is no doubt about that. Why, if the minister instituted the inquiry that is suggested in this motion great, powerful men would be affected, there is no doubt, but we would have an immediate cessation of the operations which lead to these mergers where these men make enormous sums of money and less powerful men and groups of poor people lose their all. That is what

I find in connection with this. My hon. friend stated that there had been no proof made in support of this motion that the banking facilities of the country had been injuriously affected.

Of course, the hon. gentleman (Mr. Monk), knows that he has no right to reply without the consent of- the House, as this is an amendment to go into Committee of Supply. I have no objection if the House consents.

My hon. friend (Mr. King), knows that it would not be proper to state certain particular cases here, but surely my hon. friend is aware of the details of most of these mergers, where they were engineered, what banks carried them through, and who were the individuals interested. The members of the government are supposed to know all that, the public generally know it, and it is a matter of notoriety. I think I have said enough to establish the fact that the creation of this commission would be a very useful thing.
Amendment (Mr. Monk) negatived on division and House went into Committee of Supply.
We had finished, when the House was last in Cornu Ittee of Supply-
My hon. friend (Mr. Pugsley), is not suggesting that we take up estimates to-night ?
Yes, we are going on with the Manitoba items-public buildings.
These items largely concern the city of Winnipeg and the hon. member for Winnipeg (Mr. Haggart), has gone home. It is now a quarter past eleven, and I think it is about time to discontinue work.
There is one item for Winnipeg, a military item, which I propose to allow to stand. That only leaves one item of $5,000.
The government are proposing an eight hour Bill and they should not ask us to work twelve hours a day.

I hope my hon. friend will not press the objection because we can get in an hour's work. The first item is.
Dominion public buildings-renewals, improvements, repairs &c., $15,000.
I think the minister would be well advised to let us adjourn.
I do not think so, Mr. Chairman.

I have been in this House for many years, and I have noticed that the Manitoba items usually come up
almost at midnight with the result that they are rushed through and do not get the criticism they deserve. I do not think we should be called upon to sit around here till this hour of the night waiting to have a right to protest against any of the estimates dealing with Manitoba. It is true that there are only a few items, it is true that Manitoba gets very little eon-sideraion from this government and the least consideration the Minister of Public Works might give to Manitoba, is to take up the items earlier in the day.

On days when we have set questions to be disposed of and where notice is given in advance that one of these days is intended to be used for the-purpose of discussing a question, .it is not the usual custom nor is it part of wisdom to start to do a day's work when we have reached a quarter past eleven at night. We commenced this morning at eleven o'clock with the committees and we have put in over 12 hours' work to-day.

If the hon. member for Macdonald desires to have the Manitoba items stand over I will be willing to take the items for Saskatchewan andi Alberta. The hour is quite early. I am surprised at my hon. youthful friend from East Grey wanting to go home so early.
The minister is getting along with his estimates much more rapidly than are the public buildings in Manitoba.
The sooner we get through with the estimates the more-rapidly we can do the work.
That is not my experience, the rush with the estimates is in inverse ratio to the hurry with the public buildings.
I will let the Manitoba items stand and take up Saskatchewan and Alberta. The hon. member for Macleod is here and he will be delighted to see the Macleod item go through.

Personally I do not object, but I do not think it fair to proceed in the absence of the other members from my province.
Battleford public building, $33,000.

The site has been purchased for $3,000 and the contract let. The building is for post office, &c. The contract, exclusive of heating and electric wiring, is for $26,785, and the estimated expense, including everything, is $41,310.40. Battleford, formerly the capital of the Northwest Territories, is in a fine section of country which is growing rapidly.
Is this new Battle-ford or old Battleford?
Old Battleford.
What is the population of North Battleford, and why is old Battleford chosen in preference?

Old Battleford is a considerable distance from North Battleford, and a branch line of the railway has been constructed from the main line to it. Of course a public building in North Battleford would not suit Old Battleford, and vice versa.
Old Battleford is an important place but New Battleford has also claims for a public building.
At some no distant date in the future, my hon. friend may be able to so press the claims of New Battleford that it may have a public building.
When was the contract let? ^
On the 29th of October last.
When were the plans approved?

The chief architect
tells me over a year ago.
How many tenders were received?

Tenders were called for by public advertisement. One tender was received, that of M. H. Piggott & Son, of Hamilton, for $26,735, which was nearly $12,000 below the chief architect's estimate of tire bare cost of the building. That is for the whole contract, outside of heating, lighting, fittings, lock boxes, &c.

speechtext: When did this item first appear in the estimates?
Was that before a general election or since?
My recollection is that it was before the general election.
Had it anything to do with the result?
Not that I am aware of.
Who is the representative in this House?
Mr. Champagne.
Would it not be a good thing to have the representative of the district here when such an important matter as this is being discussed.
I do not think it is essential.
Has the minister received petitions from the city council of Battleford or other public bodies urging the speedy construction of the building?

The only record I have is that application was made by Mr. Mc-Craney as long ago as January, 1907, requesting the erection of a public building in Battleford. He made out a very strong case as to the inadequacy of the present accommodation. One strong point he made was that for the offices for the different departments, the Dominion lands office, the telegrah office, the immigration hall, and the post office we were paying rents amounting to $1,536 a year.

Will the minister explain how it is, then, that without any particular urgency, except what is represented by the member for the constituency, he has given this building, while he postpones many others which were in the estimates of the same year, hut which are represented by members of the apposition?
One strong reason was that the accommodation for the various offices was wholly inadequate.
The case I have in mind has no accommodation at all.

If the accommodation was so inadequate in 1907, how is it that the work remains undone until 1911? There was urgency for the building in 1907, but there was no urgency for the next three yeai-3, and now it is getting to be urgent again.
Is my hon. friend paying the same rents now that he did in 1907? [DOT]
I presume the same.
What was the population of Battleford at the time Mr. Mc-Craney first made the suggestion?
1,800 or thereabouts.
Will the minister read to the committee the letter of recommendation he received from Mr. MoCraney?

I have not the letter, but only an epitome of it. It is dated January 19, 1907. It sets forth the rents paid for the various government offices, the amount of revenue received, money orders, &c. He states that Battleford stand's tenth in the province of Saskatchewan for gross revenue, and third for money orders paid, that each of the buildings now occupied is inadequate for the requirements of the public service, that a considerable saving in fuel and caretaking could be effected by having all the offices in one building. He also points out that Battleford is the oldest established town in Saskatchewan,

that it is a post of the Northwest Mounted Police, that it has a land office and an Indian agency, that it is destined to be a town of considerable importance, and is the centre of a fine farming country.
Is there a branch line running into old Battleford now?
You can go into both old Battleford and new Battleford by train.
Does the minister send any representatives of his department to visit these places and advise whether or not a building should be erected?
Yes, we sent a representative to chose the site.
Was he instructed to ascertain whether Liberals or Conservatives were to be served?
No.
Does he know, as a matter of fact, that his representative makes a practice of so inquiring?
I have never heard it.

Then I will give the minister an instance. Not longer ago than this summer there were certain residents of a locality not far from the city where I live who came to me with respect to certain difficulties they were in caused by floods in the Assiniboia. I am not referring now to the improvements made by the government during the month of the last election, to improvements of a similar kind undertaken by this government about 28 days before the election; but I refer to a point further east where some difficulties occurred bv reason of the flooding which could be remedied. At the request of these gentlemen I wrote the department and urged that a representative should be sent to the locality to ascertain whether or not it was the duty of the government to make similar operations in the bed of the river and thus avoid the disasters they were subject to. A petition, I believe, was also sent in. The department did send out a representative. The petition was headed by the name of a gentleman who turned out to be a staunch Liberal. The representative notified the man whose name was at the head of the petition and was met by him at the railway station and they drove together to the scene. On arriving there the representative of this government inquired what were the political complexions of those who would be benefited by the proposed alterations. He was informed by this gentleman that when they called on the representative for the constituency he made no such inquiries, but did seem to consider that the public were entitled to equal justice, no matter of what political complexion. That, however, made no impression on the representative of the Public Works Department; and having ascertained that mostly Conservatives would be benefited, he recommended, so far as my information comes from the department, that the undertaking was not such a one as should be contemplated by the department at all.
Might I ask the name of the representative of the government?

His name was Stevens, and if the hon. gentleman or the gentleman himself disputes my statement, I am prepared to give evidence in support of it at any time. I have no doubt whatever that the same practice is very rigidly adhered to in the department.
In what papers were the tenders advertised?
I am very sorry I have not got the list, but would be glad to get it, and give it to my hon. friend.

I think this item should stand. We have not got the information we are asking for, or the population of the. district in which this building is to be erected. It is now a quarter to midnight, and I think that after the effort of the ministry with regard to the eight hour Bill some attention should be paid to the comfort of the committee.
Was a contract entered into and at what price?
But we only voted $10,000, so that the department has entered into a contract $16,000 in excess of the vote.
Subject to the vote of parliament.
Is there a provision of that kind in the contract?
Yes.

It seems to me that the best reason this item should be allowed to stand is the absence of the member representing the constituency. The minister has not told us the grounds upon which he proposes to put up a building there at all. I assume he has never visited the little old village himself, and does not deign to tell us what information he has from any public official or whether he has any at all as to the necessity for this building. From the information we have, all that the minister knows in this matter he got from the gentleman who at one time represented this constituency in this House and not from t.he hon. member who represents it now. Hon. members on this side have the right to have the gentleman who *represents the constituency here so that

Hie might be subjected to cross examination regarding the statements contained in the letter which the minister says he received from the gentleman who represented the constituency at some day long past. iThe minister knows nothing about it him-feelf, and the hon. member who represents the constituency now (Mr. Champagne) is [DOT]not here. If the minister has no report Ifrom the officials of his department as to fehe necessity for a building there or as [DOT]to the character of the building, he ought not to press this item.
It seems to me that in all these eases the minister should afford members of the House information of the grounds on which he is proposing to erect a public building. In this case, the only ground the hon. gentleman gives us is a letter from a supporter and that letter is four years old. The minister has told us that circumstances change very rapidly in that new country, that cities spring up in a few hours. Four years ago there may have been need to put up a building of this kind in the place proposed, but that does not show that it may not be expedient now to expend twice as much as was then proposed. We on this side have a right to have some one here who knows the circumstances of these places, and I know no one better qualified than the gentleman who represents the constituency. But he is not here. The minister does not even tell us that he consulted the gentleman who represents the constituency.
I can tell the hon. gentleman (Mr. Crothers) now, if it will satisfy him, that on many occasions the hon. member urged upon me the need for this building.

I have no hesitation in accepting the statement of the Minister of Public Works. But the fact that the representative of the constituency urged the construction of this building is the very reason why - that representative should be here. The minister is not prepared to answer questions on cross-examination, for he has never been there, and knows nothing about it at first hand, .but all his information is at second hand from the representative of the district. But this is not the first time when the minister has asked a large sum to be spent on public buildings or on harbours and rivers when the gentleman who instigated the expenditure was not hei;e. The minister comes forward knowing nothing about it, and the member who does know about it keeps out of the chamber and gives us no opportunity to cross-examine him. I submit that this item should be allowed to stand until some one is here who is prepared to answer our questions.
This expenditure was first proposed in Mr. CROTHERS.
these estimates in 1907-8. It appears to be another of the innumerable cases provided for shortly before the last general election. I have been looking up some of the old estimates, and I find that in Nova Scotia we have had very rank illustration of that sort of thing. In the main estimates of the session before the election, the vote for harbours and rivers for Nova Scotia was about $373,000. A few months after that, it was determined to have an election; and on the 9th of July, 1908, supplementary estimates were brought down for no less a sum than $448,000 for the same purposes. Taking the two together, we find that, three months before the general election, they were giving an average of about $45,000 for each constituency of Nova Scotia. That is a nice way to endeavour to purchase a proportion of the electors in the different constituencies of that province.
Mr. Chairman, this is an item for Battleford.

Yes, and I am asking whether or not the same motive induced the putting in of this item just before the election as induced the other. And I am illustrating the evils of that system, or want of system, and would like to ascertain, as I started out by saying, from the member who represents the constituency, whether or not similar conditions exist there to those that existed in Nova Scotia, but we have not the advantage of that information, for the member for that district is not present. It is a very nice thing for the government to say, in substance, to the people of a province:	We propose to
spend $800,000 on harbours and rivers in your province before 31st March next. We are putting our candidates in a position to say to the electors of each constituency: Here is an estimate in print. The government have promised to expend, during the year ending 31st March next, in the improvement of harbours and rivers in Nova Scotia, no less a sum than $813,000. Now the election is coming on next October. If the government is sustained, these sums will be expended, if the government is not sustained, well, you take your chances of getting this money.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I admit that there are hundreds of thousands of voters in every province of this country who are not influenced by anything of that kind. I understand the answer that hon. gentlemen opposite will sometimes make: You are accusing the whole people of that province of being purchasable. Nothing of the kind. Thousands of men in the province of Nova Scotia, as in the provinces of Quebec and Ontario, are uninfluenced by any such improper motives. But I am sorry to say that in almost every constituency,

whether it be in Nova Scotia or any other province, there is a sufficient number of voters who are influenced by such improper motives to change the result of elections in that constituency. Now I would like to know from some one capable of telling us, the conditions out at Battleford. There is no one here, and we are asked to vote away $33,000 without having all the information, without being in a position to cross-examine the informant. Just fancy a minister of the Crown coming before this committee with a letter written by some one who is not here, with the person representing the constituency out of the chamber, nobody who knows anything about the conditions to answer our questions, and he asks us to vote away $33,000 for the construction of a building up ip that part of the country. I do not know whether the hon. members sitting behind the minister would vote for it if it came to a vote. We have often been asked the question: If it were proposed to erect this building in a constituency represented by the gentlemen on this side of tne House, would you oppose it? And they seem to think that there is no answer to that question. Well, Sir, if you will pardon me for referring to a personal matter, I will tell the minister that during this very session I have been requested by a number of influential electors in my constituency to try to induce the Minister of Public Works to erect a public building in a certain village. I wrote back very emphatically to them and said, I shall do nothing of the kind.
What is the name of the village?
I am not giving any names just now.
The hon. gentleman wants to keep that dark too.

I distinctly told those gentlemen that I would not be a party to asking the government to expend public money in that place, because there are many other places throughout the country very much larger and much more entitled to an expenditure of money in the public interest. I have no doubt that there are dozens of other gentlemen on this side of the House who have refused to ask the government to expend money on public buildings at places where they think it should not be expended.
I have not found many of them.
Well, I have told you the fact in regard to myself.
The hon. gentleman wont favour me even with the name of the place

No, you are not entitled to the name just now. When my
hon. friend comes to vote away public money he will then be entitled to the particulars; and if he comes to vote away any public money for the construction of a building anywhere in my constituency, and I am in the House, he will have a right to cross-examine me as to that town, just as I have a right now to cross-examine anybody who lives at Battleford. We do not know, for instance, whether this public building is intended for post office accommodation, or whether it is intended for a custom house.
The hon. gentleman must have been out when I stated what it was for. I said it was for Dominion lands office, telegraph office and post office.

The minister has told us on other occasions the exact reason why he did not put a public building in a certain town with 4,000 or 5,000 inhabitants-the post office there is now being carried on in a very commodious building, convenient to the public, for $5 a month, or $7 a month, at a much lower expendi-tur to the government than there would be if we were to expend $15,000 or $20,000 in putting up a public building. But we have no information touching that matter here. We do not know where the post office is in the old town of Battleford, we do not know how much rent is being paid for it, we do not know whether it is in a convenient position, we do not know, in a word, the very facts we ought to know, according to the minister himself, before we vote away this public money. According to his statement made on other occasions, if they have a commodious building there now, if that they are able to get at a reasonable rental in a convenient locality, then this money should not be expended. Now we have no one here to tell us the facts of the case. I submit, Mr. Chairman, that as we have already put in three quarters of an hour, and that it is past midnight, the minister ought now to accept the suggestion we made an hour ago, and not attempt to proceed with any of these items until he has some one here qualified to answer proper and legitimate questions submitted by hon. members on this side of the House.

I must submit with the utmost deference, that I do not think the minister has given us reasons why we should vote this sum of money. I find in examining the report of the Postmaster General of last year some rather interesting facts. For example, I find that the postal revenue for the town of Battleford was the sum of $4,246.81. Upon looking at the return for the town of North Battleford, which I believe is at a distance of some seven miles away, the postal revenue was $5,226.97, or something like one-fifth more. Then of money orders issued in the

town of Battleford, the return is $3,078; in the town of North Battleford, $5,604. In the next column I find that the total amount of money orders issued was for the town of Battleford, $33,900.36; the total amount of money orders issued to the town of North Battleford comprised the sum ot $71,351.80, or in round numbers more than double. Again, the total commission received from the public in the town of Battleford was $213.08, and for the town of North Battleford, $425.85. Again, in the next column the number of money orders paid shows a slight increase in the case of [DOT]North Battleford. The same with the total amount of (postal notes paid. Again, the compensation paid to the postmaster in the [DOT]town of Battleford was $137.69, that is, I (believe, has percentage in addition to the 'salary; in North Battleford it was $238.81. 'Now all these instances go to show that in North Battleford you have a larger and 'more flourishing town, but you give the public building to Battleford. Take, for 'instance, the volume of the money orders in Battleford, $33,000; in North Battleford, '$71,000. It would be only fair for the Minister of Public Works to take us into his 'confidence and tell us why it is that old 'Battleford has been chosen for the site 'of this post office, rather than North Battleford. It would be doing simple justice 'to the citizens of North Battleford to let 'them know why old Battleford is chosen in preference.
1 Mr. PUGSLEY. I should be very glad indeed to give my hon. friend that information, but if we had to let items stand 'because the member for the constituency 'did not happen to be present, we would *not be able to get on with the business. It does not make any more difference to 'me than hon. gentlemen opposite whether they talk against time or whether they do not, but I think it makes a little difference to the people of the country. I want to congratulate my hon. friend in my eye Qn talking against time while apparently conveying the impression to many who listened to him that he was not doing so. I have heard a great many public (men in my day in the legislature where I attended for a number of years doing the same thing, but I have never heard one who does it more admirably than my hon. friend who is just in front of me. But he ought to remember that it costs a little, that every half hour that we take up unnecessarily here costs something to the country and I do not believe my hon. friend will approve of it. The question is simply whether we shall vote an item to enable the department to pay the contractors for this building to which parliament has already committed itself. Is it worth while to waste time simply for the sake of wasting time ? With regard to the reason Mr. RHODES.
asked for, very courteously, by the hon. imember for Cumberland (Mr. Rhodes), with whom I have no fault to find, because he did not follow the example of the hon. gentleman who preceded him, tihe reason why we selected Battleford is, that this is an old town and it is growing, not rapidly, but it is growing very well indeed. While the main line of the.Canadian Northern railway passed it by, it has now been connected up with a branch line and I believe both the Grand Trunk Pacific land the Canadian Pacific railway have Old Battleford in view and are seeking approval of routes by which they propose to reach that town. Battleford, according to my own observation, is in the centre of a magnificent, a beautiful farming country, first class settlers have gone in there and it happens that in old Battleford we have several departments of the government. We have the Immigration Department, the Mounted Police, a telegraph office, a Dominion Lands office, and for all these we are paying a pretty heavy rental. The accommodation is not what it ought to be and it will be very muijh better to have these different departments housed in one building.
What rental does the minister pay?

We are paying $1,536. Surely it is better to pass this item, and I will only ask for two or three more, including Macleod. Then, we will be able to go home to our comfortable beds and have the consciousness that we have done some actual work.

I desire to say one word in reply to the minister. If I had not sat here for two sessions and listened to his persuasive and comforting voice I would be amazed at the courage he has displayed on this occasion in charging me with talking at this hour of the night and wasting time. I want to resent that statement with all the seriousness and indignation of which I am capable. Members of the House know very well that I very seldom take up any time in addressing the House. I think I may fairly claim credit for that. I never take up any time unless I feel that I have something to say. Every hon. member present I think, will admit that while I have had the honour of a seat in this House. I have taken up comparatively little time in discussing public matters. But, it does not become the hon. minister as a member of this House to accuse any other member of talking against time. I desire anything I have to say in this House to be adjudged upon its merits, and in my judgment hon. members who heard what I said a few minutes ago will agree with what I say.
The majority would be against you now.

When the minister was requested at half-past eleven to adjourn he refused to do so and now talks about hon. members wasting time. He ill-estimates the opinion of the people of this country when he .does not know that the universal opinion is that we are putting in too much time after twelve o'clock, that honest and virtuous men ought to be in their beds before twelve o'clock and that the business of this country would be better performed if we concluded at ten o'clock at night, if we should go to bed at that hour and come back next day and work in daylight and not at night. It has been said by members of this" House and by hundreds of -eonle outside of this House, that the sitting's of the House are too protracted during the night. They are surprised at the hour at which these estimates are going through and especially on Friday night, when a great many members are away. The general opinion is that these estimates go through at these late hours with the deliberate intention of putting them, through the House when non. members, exhausted by the lon<* hours, have gone home. That is the opinion of the public outside of this House and yet the minister has the courage to get up at a quarter-past twelve and accuse an hon. member of wasting the time of_ the country by talking about these expenditures and insisting upon the committee adjourning that we may go home and go to bed like the honest, virtuous politicians we all claim to be The minister would stand higher in the estimation of the electors of the country if he came before this House in daylight and asked for these estimates then instead of coming to the House at twelve o'clock at night, or one, two or three in the morning, and getting estimates through after the members of this House, by reason of these long hours, have become exhausted and gone home to recuperate in order that they may be enabled to fight next day. The attack which the hon. gentleman made on me was entirely uncalled for.
I was congratulating you.
You cannot-I was going to say-humbug me, as the minister attempts to humbug others by any such sweet words as those. I submit that at this hour the committee had better adjourn.

I was surprised to hear the minister state in one breath that from personal observation he could assure the House of the character of the country
around Battleford when in the next breath he told us he had never 'been there.
I said I had passed through North Battleford, and that I saw there one of the most beautiful sections of country my eyes ever rested on.

Then his eyes deceived him. The soil there is so sandy that when portions of the Mo-osomin reserve within a few miles of the town were put up at auction they could not get a ibid at any price, and yet the minister tells us from personal observation it is the finest country his eyes ever rested on.

I submit that the sitting member of the county should be present when an important item as this is being discussed. I make that submission because on one occasion I remember a supporter of the government condemning the government for uselessly voting public money in his constituency, and perhaps the member for this constituency would do the same thing.	[DOT]
My hon. friend need have no fear of that.
You never can tell. The sitting member for the county on that occasion condemned the government for the expenditure.
Who was the member?
Mr. McEwan who represented Huron some years ago.
There has been no such member since I have been here.
And there is no such disposition now.

I have no doubt that such a thing 'would surprise the Minister of Public Works because he has educated his followers in a different method. But the fact is that Mr. McEwren denounced an expenditure on a wharf at St. Joseph in his county, and refused to he held responsible for it, and ,$15,000 were wasted there, and all you can see to-day is a few posts sticking out of the water, and no sign of a wharf. In view of such an incident as that surely the sitting member for the constituency ought to be here. I would like to know whether there has been any correspondence 'between the sitting member and the minister with respect to putting this item in the estimates.
I have given a summary of that correspondence.

My complaint is that my hon. friend, ,instead of bringing down to the committee the letters recommending this building, leaves them in the department. I take the ground that all the correspondence respecting an item of this

kind ought to he forthcoming. My hon. friend refused to bring down original documents. If he brought them down, I am quite sure there would be less criticism, and he would be able to get his items passed through the committee much more quickly.

I am so much impressed with the forcible argument of my hon. friend, and his thirst for information that I feel disposed to accede to the very strong desire he has expressed that the item stand over till to-morrow ; 'and when that thirst is satisfied by the production of the letters, I understand that he will assist me in getting this item through.
Progress reported.
